Quarterly engine: line-level NII on sector yields and costs, a laddered receive-fixed hedge at actual ZAR swap fixings (3m JIBAR, then compounded ZARONIA + 16.19 bp CAS from 2027Q1), sector credit-loss ratio with relative multipliers, CET1 with the FVOCI reserve, LCR/NSFR proxies calibrated to PA aggregates. The deposit series ([one](/posts/deposit-beta-1-4/), [two](/posts/deposit-duration-2-4/), [three](/posts/hedge-optim-3-4/), [four](/posts/pricing-unknown-4-4/)) ended with No Gut Feelings Bank's funding understood about as well as public data allow. Balances that do not run off. Betas that separate cleanly by product. A structural hedge whose size follows from those betas rather than from an argument. And a run that cannot be estimated from the returns, so it was priced instead. All four posts were about one side of the balance sheet, and all four took the economy as given.

An ALCO gets to do neither. Every quarter the macro pack arrives (the house view, an upside, a downside, sometimes a scenario the regulator has asked for) and the committee asks the same three questions of it. How exposed are we? What does each scenario do to our returns? What should we do before it arrives? There is a fourth question that rarely makes the pack, because it is uncomfortable: what should we do when we do not know which scenario is coming? Which is always.

Most banks own the machinery to answer them, and point it at something else. Macro models in a bank usually live with the stress-testing team: they turn the regulator's adverse scenario into a capital ratio for the internal capital adequacy assessment (ICAAP) and supply the forward-looking scenarios behind the IFRS 9 credit provisions. Once a year they prove that the bank survives something unpleasant, and then they go back in the cabinet with the good crockery. That undersells them. A model that can say what a recession does to capital can say what any macro path does to every line of the balance sheet, which makes it useful every quarter, for three jobs a stress test never asks of it:

* **Strategy.** Which balance-sheet decisions (the hedge, the liquidity book, the bond portfolio, the payout) depend on a macro view and which do not, and what each is worth either way.
* **Performance against the market.** A business that grew its book 8% while its market grew 12% lost ground, however well 8% presents at bonus time. Take the market's growth out of each segment's and what is left is what management actually did.
* **What is reasonable to expect.** What the card book, the home loans or the deposit franchise can deliver in each scenario, given its market and how a typical bank behaves in that phase of the cycle. A target becomes arithmetic rather than a negotiation, and the ALCO knows in advance which segments will look bad next year for reasons that are not their fault.

This post puts the machinery to all three jobs for NGFB, with public SARB data and nothing else, and answers the four questions on the way. It gives the bank the rest of its balance sheet, ties the economy to the industry and the industry to the bank, and runs the result through three scenarios and then through `r RB$n_episodes` replayed windows of South African history since 2008. The answers are less flattering to forecasting than ALCO packs usually are. NGFB's hedge turns out to be a rate bet. Positioning ahead of a downside recovers a sliver of the damage and costs more than it earns if you are wrong. Across sixty-odd histories, timing the rate cycle earns nothing on average. What pays is collecting premia that need no view at all, and choosing every lever together under an explicit risk budget lifts NGFB's average ROE from `r pct(plan_roe)` to `r pct(plan_roe + cen$d_roe)`, beating its plan in every one of the histories. Then there is one more lever, which the optimiser did not have until I went looking for it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-headline
#| fig-cap: "Where two points of ROE come from. Each bar is a lever's contribution to NGFB's three-year average ROE, averaged over the replayed histories, against the bank's plan. The two spread trades in the middle need no view on rates."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.9
#| code-summary: "Figure: the headline bridge"
ra <- rg["All episodes", ]
wf <- data.frame(
  lab = c("Plan", "Hedge ratio\nand tenor", "Ten-year\nbonds", "Asset-swapped\nbonds", "Smaller\nbuffer",
          "Payout\nrule", "Interaction", "Risk-budgeted\nportfolio", "Repo-funded\ncarry", "With the\ncarry book"),
  val = 1e4 * c(0, ra$hedge, ra$dur, ra$as, ra$buf, ra$pay, ra$interaction, cen$d_roe, cyr$d_roe_vs_central, cyr$d_roe),
  kind = c("level", rep("step", 6), "level", "step", "level"))
cum <- 0; wf$lo <- wf$hi <- NA
for (i in seq_len(nrow(wf))) {
  if (wf$kind[i] == "level") { wf$lo[i] <- 0; wf$hi[i] <- wf$val[i]; cum <- wf$val[i] }
  else { wf$lo[i] <- cum; wf$hi[i] <- cum + wf$val[i]; cum <- cum + wf$val[i] }
}
wf$x <- seq_len(nrow(wf)); wf$lab <- factor(wf$lab, levels = wf$lab)
wf$fill <- ifelse(wf$kind == "level", MUTE, ifelse(wf$val >= 0, ACCENT, WARN))
wf$fill[wf$x == 9] <- ACCENT2
wf$txt <- ifelse(wf$kind == "level", sprintf("%.0f", wf$hi), sprintf("%+.0f", wf$val))
wf$txt[1] <- sprintf("%.1f%%\nROE", 100 * plan_roe)
ggplot(wf) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = x - .38, xmax = x + .38, ymin = pmin(lo, hi), ymax = pmax(lo, hi), fill = fill), alpha = .92) +
  geom_segment(data = wf[-nrow(wf), ], aes(x = x + .38, xend = x + .62, y = hi, yend = hi), colour = MUTE, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_text(aes(x = x, y = pmax(lo, hi) + 7, label = txt), colour = FG, size = 3.3, vjust = 0, lineheight = .9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = wf$x, labels = levels(wf$lab), expand = expansion(add = .4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-15, 265), breaks = seq(0, 250, 50)) +
  labs(title = "Where two points of ROE come from",
       subtitle = sprintf("Change in NGFB's three-year average ROE against its plan (%.1f%%), averaged over %d replayed macro histories, bps",
                          100 * plan_roe, RB$n_episodes),
       x = NULL, y = "bps of ROE") +
  theme_slate() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9, lineheight = .9), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

Most of that comes from two trades that would look dull in a board pack, and the dullness is the point. Neither depends on where the repo rate goes. The rest of this post builds up to that result one piece at a time, because every piece turned out to matter, including the ones that went wrong.

## From the macro to one bank, in two stages

The obvious way to tie a bank to the economy is to regress the bank's numbers on macro variables. It is also a reliable way to produce nonsense. A single bank's history is short, and it is full of things that are not the economy: an acquisition, a new strategy, a provisioning overlay, a curatorship. Regress that on GDP and you get elasticities that are unstable and, more often than is comfortable, the wrong sign. It is like judging a flyhalf's form by the rand–dollar exchange rate. There will be a correlation, and you will regret acting on it.

So the macro relationships are estimated once, on the industry, where the economy is the main thing moving the numbers, and the bank is modelled relative to the industry. For any product $p$, the identity

$$g^{\text{bank}}_{p,t} \;=\; g^{\text{sector}}_{p,t} \;+\; \Delta \log s_{p,t}$$

splits the bank's growth in quarter $t$ into two pieces. Growth $g$ is measured in logs so that the pieces add rather than multiply, and $s_{p,t}$ is the bank's market share of product $p$. The first piece is how fast the whole market grew. The second is how much faster or slower than the market the bank grew, which is exactly the change in its market share. Being an identity, it cannot be wrong. What it does is split one hard problem into two tractable ones. How the industry responds to the economy is where the macro lives. Whether this bank gains or loses ground, and when, is where the bank lives.

**Stage 1** maps a macro path to the industry: the growth of each loan and deposit book, lending spreads over prime and the three-month benchmark, deposit costs, the credit-loss ratio, fees and operating costs. That is `r M$n_sector_models` series in all, built on the SARB's BA900 and BA100/BA120 returns [@SARB2025BA900]. The workhorse is a sign-restricted ARDL model, and that is all I am going to say about it here. Its specification, its estimates and how it was chosen are staying in the drawer for now, like any koeksister recipe worth having. For this post it is a black box with a simple contract: hand it a macro path, and it hands back the industry's volumes, margins and losses along that path.

One design choice matters for everything that follows. **Nothing in this post forecasts the economy.** Every macro path, whether a scenario or a slice of history, is taken as given, and the only question is what it does to the bank. That is deliberate. An ALCO will argue about which scenario is coming whatever any model says. The model's job is to make sure everyone is arguing about the same consequences.

**Stage 2** is the bank's part, and it is simple enough to write down in full. For each peer group and product, the annualised change in log market share is

$$400\,\Delta \log s_t \;=\; a \;+\; \delta_{\text{c}}\,C_t \;+\; \delta_{\text{h}}\,H_t \;+\; \delta_{\text{e}}\,E_t \;+\; \kappa\,\big(g^{\text{sector}}_t - \bar g\big) \;+\; e_t .$$

Read it left to right. The 400 turns a quarterly change in log share into percentage points a year: four quarters, times a hundred. $a$ is the structural drift, how fast the group gains or loses share in an ordinary quarter, which for some groups is a decade-long march summarised in one number. $C_t$, $H_t$ and $E_t$ are switches that turn on in contraction, hiking and easing quarters, so each $\delta$ is the extra drift in that regime compared with a neutral quarter. The $\kappa$ term asks whether the group grows faster than the market when the market is booming, meaning sector growth $g^{\text{sector}}_t$ above its average $\bar g$, and slower when it is not. $\kappa > 0$ is a pro-cyclical share. $e_t$ is everything else: a new app, a new chief executive, a weekend the core banking system spent offline.

The regimes are defined mechanically, with contraction taking priority. A quarter is a contraction if real GDP is lower than a year earlier. Otherwise it is hiking or easing if the repo rate has moved up or down by at least 25 bps over two quarters, and otherwise it is neutral. Since 2008 that gives `r nreg[["contraction"]]` contraction quarters, `r nreg[["hiking"]]` hiking, `r nreg[["easing"]]` easing and `r nreg[["neutral"]]` neutral.

```{r}
#| label: fig-regimes
#| fig-cap: "The macro regimes behind Stage 2. Contraction takes priority (real GDP below a year earlier); then hiking or easing (the repo rate up or down at least 25 bps over two quarters); otherwise neutral."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| code-summary: "Figure: regimes"
rp <- S$stage2$regime_path
rp$reg <- factor(tools::toTitleCase(rp$regime), levels = c("Contraction", "Hiking", "Easing", "Neutral"))
ru <- rle(as.character(rp$reg)); ends <- cumsum(ru$lengths); starts <- ends - ru$lengths + 1
runs <- data.frame(reg = factor(ru$values, levels = levels(rp$reg)), start = rp$date[starts] - 91, end = rp$date[ends])
ggplot(rp) +
  geom_rect(data = runs[runs$reg != "Neutral", ], aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = reg), alpha = .30) +
  geom_line(aes(date, repo), colour = FG, linewidth = .9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Contraction = WARN, Hiking = ACCENT2, Easing = ACCENT), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = "Eighteen years of South African monetary and business cycles",
       subtitle = sprintf("Repo rate, with the regimes shaded (unshaded = neutral). %d contraction, %d hiking, %d easing and %d neutral quarters.",
                          nreg[["contraction"]], nreg[["hiking"]], nreg[["easing"]], nreg[["neutral"]]),
       x = NULL, y = "repo rate") +
  theme_slate()
```

Real banks only ever appear pooled, in peer groups with at least four members in every quarter. The Big Four are the universal banks that have dominated South African banking for decades. The Challengers are the retail and digital banks that have taken share since 2008. The Specialists are business, private-client, Islamic and community banks, and everyone else is Other.

The bank layer needs more than peer-group averages, though, because NGFB has to be a plausible *single* bank. So the six large banks' equations are estimated one by one and pooled into a population with a random-effects estimator [@DerSimonianLaird1986]. Each bank's estimate $\hat\theta_b$ of a parameter is treated as the population mean, plus the bank's genuine difference from it, plus estimation noise:

$$\hat\theta_b \;=\; \mu \;+\; u_b \;+\; \varepsilon_b, \qquad u_b \sim N(0,\tau^2), \qquad \varepsilon_b \sim N(0,\mathrm{se}_b^2).$$

The noise variances are known, because every estimate comes with its standard error. So whatever spread between the banks' estimates is left over beyond what noise can explain is genuine difference between banks, $\tau^2$. DerSimonian and Laird estimate it by the method of moments, and the population mean $\mu$ is then a weighted average that trusts the precisely estimated banks more than the noisy ones. NGFB's parameters are a draw for a new member of that population, from $N(\mu,\,\tau^2 + \mathrm{se}_\mu^2)$: the population mean, spread by both the genuine differences between banks and the uncertainty about the mean itself. The draw is truncated to the same central probability mass the deposit posts used, which keeps NGFB typical. NGFB's own structural drift is then switched off. A drawn drift of a few percent a year compounds into large and arbitrary share gains over three years, and the question here is how NGFB responds to the cycle, not whether it can out-grow the market by decree.

```{r}
#| label: fig-drifts
#| fig-cap: "Structural share drift by peer group, 2008–2026: the change in log market share in a neutral quarter, in percentage points a year, with two standard errors either side."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-summary: "Figure: who has been taking share"
dr <- cg[cg$param == "(Intercept)" & cg$product %in% names(PROD_LAB), ]
dr$se <- ifelse(abs(dr$t) > 1e-9, abs(dr$est / dr$t), NA)
dr$prod <- factor(PROD_LAB[dr$product], levels = rev(PROD_LAB[c("cards", "personal_other", "mortgages_res", "corp_all", "nmd", "dep_retail", "beh_term")]))
dr <- dr[!is.na(dr$prod), ]
dr$entity <- factor(dr$entity, levels = c("Big Four", "Challengers", "Specialists"))
pd <- position_dodge(width = .62)
ggplot(dr, aes(est, prod, colour = entity)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = est - 2 * se, xmax = est + 2 * se), height = 0, linewidth = .6, position = pd, alpha = .75) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, position = pd) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Big Four` = ACCENT, Challengers = ACCENT2, Specialists = INDIGO), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-30, 30)) +
  labs(title = "Who has been taking share since 2008",
       subtitle = "Structural drift a, pp of market share growth a year. The Challengers' gains are large and significant; the Big Four's losses small but steady.",
       x = "pp a year", y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

The drifts carry the clearest message in the share data. Over 2008–2026 the Challengers took share at double-digit rates in credit cards (`r sprintf("%+.1f", drift("Challengers", "cards"))` pp a year, $t$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", drift("Challengers", "cards", "t"))`), household deposits (`r sprintf("%+.1f", drift("Challengers", "dep_retail"))`, $t$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", drift("Challengers", "dep_retail", "t"))`) and non-maturity deposits (`r sprintf("%+.1f", drift("Challengers", "nmd"))`, $t$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", drift("Challengers", "nmd", "t"))`). The Big Four ceded share slowly but steadily in cards, household deposits and home loans. The regime effects are mostly imprecise, which is what eleven contraction quarters buy you: plenty of misery, not much precision. It is why they are pooled across banks and truncated before they reach NGFB rather than trusted bank by bank.

## NGFB gets the rest of a balance sheet

The deposit posts only needed NGFB's deposits. This one needs everything, so NGFB inherits what the series fixed and gets the rest by the same rule: a typical large South African bank, drawn from the population, never a copy of any one of them.

What carries over is the deposit franchise. The mix of operational, notice, savings and term deposits (`r paste(paste(sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * dep_mix[1:3]), collapse = ", "), "and", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * dep_mix[4]))`), the product-level betas, the structural hedge at `r pct(N$hedge_ratio)` of non-maturity deposits received fixed in a five-year rolling ladder, and Post 3's bridge from interest-earning assets to equity.

What is new is everything else. NGFB's size is the average of the six largest banks: `r rbn(N$ta)` of assets, `r pct(N$ta / N$sector_ta)` of the BA900 sector at 2026Q2. Its asset mix is drawn from the population of the same six banks, and that draw needs one piece of machinery worth explaining, because balance-sheet shares are awkward objects. They are positive and they add up to one, so you cannot put a normal distribution on them directly: a normal draw would happily produce negative mortgages. The standard fix is the additive log-ratio transform [@Aitchison1986]. Divide every share by a reference share and take logs,

$$z_k \;=\; \log\frac{w_k}{w_K}, \qquad k = 1,\dots,K-1,$$

which turns $K$ shares that must add to one into $K-1$ unconstrained numbers. Fit a multivariate normal to the six banks' $z$'s, draw from it, and transform back. Every draw is then a valid balance sheet. Six banks cannot pin down the covariance of eleven product shares, which would be 66 parameters from six observations, so the draw is made over six business lines (five dimensions) and products are split within each line at the population's average mix.

The draw is truncated by its Mahalanobis distance from the population centre,

$$d \;=\; \sqrt{(z-\mu)^{\top}\,\Sigma^{-1}\,(z-\mu)} \;\le\; r ,$$

which measures how far a draw sits from the centre in units that allow for the spread and correlation of the population: in one dimension, $d = 1$ is one standard deviation. The radius $r$ = `r num(N$radius, 2)` keeps the same central probability mass in five dimensions as the deposit draw's radius of 1 did in three. NGFB lands at $d$ = `r num(N$distance, 2)`, comfortably inside.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mix
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's business-line mix against the population centre. Inside the truncation radius overall, but with more than twice the centre's unsecured lending."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| code-summary: "Figure: the asset draw"
ml <- c(retail_secured = "Retail secured", retail_unsecured = "Retail unsecured", corporate = "Corporate",
        treasury = "Treasury", hqla = "HQLA", other = "Other assets")
mx <- rbind(data.frame(line = names(mix), v = mix, who = "NGFB"), data.frame(line = names(mixc), v = mixc, who = "Population centre"))
mx$line <- factor(ml[mx$line], levels = rev(ml)); mx$who <- factor(mx$who, levels = c("Population centre", "NGFB"))
ggplot(mx, aes(v, line, fill = who)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = .72), width = .66, alpha = .92) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * v)), position = position_dodge(width = .72), hjust = -.15, colour = FG, size = 3.1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(NGFB = ACCENT, `Population centre` = MUTE), name = NULL, breaks = c("NGFB", "Population centre")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, .34)) +
  labs(title = "Typical on the whole, not typical line by line",
       subtitle = sprintf("Share of total assets. Mahalanobis distance %.2f against a truncation radius of %.2f.", N$distance, N$radius),
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

Typical on the whole is not typical line by line. The seed puts NGFB on the unsecured side of the population, with retail unsecured lending at `r pct(mix[["retail_unsecured"]])` of assets against the centre's `r pct(mixc[["retail_unsecured"]])`. That is a legitimate member of the population, since one of the six large banks is an unsecured specialist, and it is kept because the seed is canonical. Rerolling a seed until you like the bank is how audit findings are born. It colours everything that follows. NGFB holds `r pct(nsh[["cards"]], 0)` of the industry's credit cards and `r pct(nsh[["personal_other"]], 0)` of its personal loans, against `r pct(nsh[["mortgages_res"]], 0)` of home loans, and its credit-loss ratio sits well above the sector's.

NGFB is *added* to the industry rather than carved out of it, the convention the deposit posts used. Real banks keep their own books, market shares are measured against the sector plus NGFB, and NGFB's history is back-cast with its drawn share parameters, so that it lives through 2008–2026 the way a bank with those parameters would have.

Prices, losses and costs exist only at sector level, because BA900 is the only return published per bank. So NGFB is priced with the sector's own yields, deposit costs, loss ratio and cost ratios, and the parameters nobody publishes are solved for rather than assumed. The wholesale funding spread, `r num(N$wholesale_spread, 2)` pp over the three-month benchmark, is the one that makes the engine's net interest income on the sector's balance sheet match what BA120 reports for the last four quarters. The liquidity run-off scalars are the ones that reproduce the sector LCR of `r pct(N$lcr_sector)` and NSFR of `r pct(N$nsfr_sector)` that the Prudential Authority publishes [@PA2025Trends]. NGFB starts with a CET1 ratio of `r pct(N$cet1_0)`, an LCR of `r pct(N$lcr_1, 0)` and an NSFR of `r pct(N$nsfr_1, 0)`: more liquid than the sector, because it holds more HQLA and less wholesale funding.

## The engine

Each quarter the engine does what a bank's planning model does, line by line. Every book grows with the industry's growth for that product, adjusted by NGFB's share dynamics, and wholesale funding balances the books, which is what a bank actually does at the margin. Then comes the income statement, starting with net interest income:

$$\text{NII}_t \;=\; \sum_{i\,\in\,\text{assets}} \bar B_{i,t}\,\frac{y_{i,t}}{4} \;-\; \sum_{j\,\in\,\text{liabilities}} \bar B_{j,t}\,\frac{c_{j,t}}{4} \;+\; H_t .$$

That is average balance $\bar B$ times rate, a quarter at a time, for every asset (at yield $y$) and every liability (at cost $c$), plus $H_t$, the structural hedge's net settlement. Loans earn prime or the three-month benchmark plus the industry's projected spreads, deposits cost the industry's projected deposit costs, and HQLA earns roughly the Treasury bill rate. The hedge term deserves its own line, because it is where most of this post's money is made and lost:

$$H_t \;=\; \sum_{i} N_i\,\frac{F_i - f_t}{4} .$$

Each tranche $i$ of the receive-fixed hedge earns its fixed rate $F_i$ and pays the floating benchmark $f_t$ on its notional $N_i$. One twentieth of the book matures every quarter and is replaced at the then five-year swap rate, so the book's average fixed rate drifts slowly while the floating rate moves at the speed of the Monetary Policy Committee. The gap between the two is the hedge carry, and it is the whole story of how a structural hedge makes or loses money.

Below NII the engine is plain accounting, the part nobody presents at conferences and every number depends on:

$$\text{NI}_t \;=\; (1-\tau)\big(\text{NII}_t + \text{NIR}_t - \text{Opex}_t - \text{Imp}_t\big), \qquad \text{ROE}_t \;=\; \frac{4\,\text{NI}_t}{\tfrac12\,(E_{t-1}+E_t)} .$$

Fees ($\text{NIR}$) and operating costs follow the industry's ratios to assets. Impairments are the industry's credit-loss ratio scaled up or down by product, unsecured highest and home loans lowest, because no return publishes losses by product. Net income is profit after tax at rate $\tau$. Half of it is paid out and the rest retained, so equity rolls forward as $E_t = E_{t-1} + \text{NI}_t - \text{dividends}_t$, and ROE is annualised net income over average equity. The CET1 ratio is CET1 over risk-weighted assets, and the LCR and NSFR are proxies built from BA900's depositor-by-maturity matrix. Every ROE in this post is the average over the twelve quarters from 2026Q3 to 2029Q2.

One more piece of plumbing has become topical. JIBAR, the three-month rate that floating loans, wholesale funding and the hedge's floating leg have referenced for a generation, publishes its last fixing on 31 December 2026 [@SARB2025JIBARCessation], so somebody in every treasury already knows how they are spending New Year's Eve. From 2027Q1 the engine's floating benchmark is compounded ZARONIA plus the fixed 16.19 bp fallback spread, so `r nw(tr$n_post)` of the twelve projected quarters are priced off JIBAR's successor. More on what that does further down.

## Three scenarios, and who wins in each

| Scenario | What happens | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Inflation peaks above 5% around the turn of the year and is back at the 3% target by late 2027. The repo rate holds at 7.25%, then eases gradually to a neutral 6.25%. Growth settles at about 1.6%. | `r pct(wts[["baseline"]], 0)` |
| **Upside:** faster disinflation and a growth dividend | Oil and food prices ease and inflation reaches the target early. The SARB cuts a further 100 bps, terms-of-trade gains and electricity and logistics reform lift growth to about 3%, the rand firms and the long bond rallies about 100 bps. | `r pct(wts[["upside"]], 0)` |
| **Downside:** stagflationary shock | A fiscal slippage and a rand sell-off push inflation above 6%. The SARB hikes a further 150 bps and the long bond sells off about 200 bps. The economy contracts for two years, unemployment rises 2.5 points and house prices fall. | `r pct(wts[["downside"]], 0)` |
| **Downside with cuts** (variant) | The same contraction, but inflation falls and the SARB cuts 150 bps instead of hiking. | – |

The baseline starts from the realised data at 2026Q2 and follows the SARB's own guidance for the year ahead: the repo rate at 7.25% after the September 2026 increase, inflation above 5% around the turn of the year and back at the 3% target (adopted, with a one-point tolerance band, in November 2025) by late 2027. The upside and the downside are shocks layered on top, with build-up, hold and decay profiles, and everything derived from them (prime, the floating benchmark, the curve's slope, swap rates) is recomputed so that every path hangs together.

The downside is deliberately stagflationary. The SARB built the domestic adverse scenario of its 2023 common stress test the same way: a higher country risk premium and a sharply weaker rand push inflation up, the SARB tightens, bond yields reprice and the economy contracts [@SARB2023FSR]. The other kind of recession, demand-led, with inflation falling and the SARB cutting as in 2009 and 2020, is run as a variant with the same real shock. For a hedged bank, as the numbers below show, the policy response decides the sign of the rate effect.

```{r}
#| label: fig-paths
#| fig-cap: "The macro paths, with history in grey. The dashed line is the downside's variant with rate cuts; the variant shares the downside's GDP path."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| code-summary: "Figure: the scenarios"
vl <- c(repo = "Repo rate (%)", gdp_yy = "Real GDP growth, y/y (%)", cpi_yy = "CPI inflation, y/y (%)", gov10y = "10-year government yield (%)")
hp <- S$scen$hist; spth <- S$scen$paths
long <- function(d, who) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(vl), function(v) data.frame(date = d$date, var = vl[[v]], v = d[[v]], who = who)))
hl <- long(hp, "History")
sl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spth, spth$scenario), function(d) long(d, SC_LAB[[d$scenario[1]]])))
jo <- hp[hp$date == max(hp$date), ]
sl <- rbind(sl, do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(sl$who), function(w) long(jo, w))))   # join each path to the jump-off
sl$who <- factor(sl$who, levels = names(SC_COL)); hl$var <- factor(hl$var, levels = vl); sl$var <- factor(sl$var, levels = vl)
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = hl, aes(date, v), colour = MUTE, linewidth = .7) +
  geom_line(data = sl, aes(date, v, colour = who, linetype = who), linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~var, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = SC_COL, name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Baseline = "solid", Upside = "solid", Downside = "solid", `Downside with cuts` = "22"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Three scenarios and a variant", subtitle = "Quarterly paths from the 2026Q2 jump-off to 2029Q2", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

Here is what the engine makes of them, as three-year averages.

| Scenario | NGFB ROE | against the baseline | Net income, 3 years | NGFB without its hedge | Sector ROE | CET1 trough |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | `r pct(st["baseline", "ngfb"])` | – | `r rbn(st["baseline", "ni"], 1)` | `r pct(st["baseline", "ngfb_nohedge"])` | `r pct(st["baseline", "sector"])` | `r pct(st["baseline", "cet1_min"])` |
| Upside | `r pct(st["upside", "ngfb"])` | `r bps(st["upside", "ngfb"] - st["baseline", "ngfb"])` | `r rbn(st["upside", "ni"], 1)` | `r pct(st["upside", "ngfb_nohedge"])` | `r pct(st["upside", "sector"])` | `r pct(st["upside", "cet1_min"])` |
| Downside | `r pct(st["downside", "ngfb"])` | `r bps(st["downside", "ngfb"] - st["baseline", "ngfb"])` | `r rbn(st["downside", "ni"], 1)` | `r pct(st["downside", "ngfb_nohedge"])` | `r pct(st["downside", "sector"])` | `r pct(st["downside", "cet1_min"])` |
| Downside with cuts | `r pct(st["downside_cuts", "ngfb"])` | `r bps(st["downside_cuts", "ngfb"] - st["baseline", "ngfb"])` | `r rbn(st["downside_cuts", "ni"], 1)` | `r pct(st["downside_cuts", "ngfb_nohedge"])` | `r pct(st["downside_cuts", "sector"])` | `r pct(st["downside_cuts", "cet1_min"])` |

To see where each difference comes from, the engine swaps one block of inputs at a time from the baseline into the scenario: volumes (the growth paths), pricing (rates, yields and deposit costs, and with them the hedge), credit (the loss ratio), and fees and costs. Whatever remains when all four are swapped together is the interaction, so the bars always add up to the total. The sector is run through the same engine, unhedged.

```{r}
#| label: fig-attribution
#| fig-cap: "Where each scenario's ROE effect comes from, for NGFB and for the BA900 sector run through the same engine without a hedge. Bars add up to the total."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-summary: "Figure: attribution"
chl <- c(volume = "Volume", pricing = "Pricing\n(incl. hedge)", credit = "Credit", fees_costs = "Fees and\ncosts", total = "Total")
ad <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(chl), function(ch) data.frame(scenario = at$scenario, entity = at$entity, ch = chl[[ch]], v = 1e4 * at[[ch]])))
ad$scenario <- factor(SC_LAB[ad$scenario], levels = SC_LAB[c("upside", "downside", "downside_cuts")])
ad$ch <- factor(ad$ch, levels = chl); ad$entity <- factor(ad$entity, levels = c("NGFB", "Sector"))
ggplot(ad, aes(ch, v, fill = entity)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = .74), width = .68, alpha = .92) +
  facet_wrap(~scenario, ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(NGFB = ACCENT, Sector = MUTE), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The sector is an endowment play; NGFB is a credit play",
       subtitle = "Change in three-year average ROE against the baseline, by channel, bps",
       x = NULL, y = "bps of ROE") +
  theme_slate() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8.5, lineheight = .9), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

**The industry is an endowment play.** Deposits and equity are cheap funding that a bank lends out at market rates, so when rates rise, it earns more on them [@Drechsler2021Banking]. Without a hedge, the higher repo path in the downside adds `r bps(att("downside", "Sector", "pricing"))` to the sector's ROE through pricing and more than offsets its credit losses (`r bps(att("downside", "Sector", "credit"))`). In the upside, the cuts take `r ubps(att("upside", "Sector", "pricing"))` away and better credit only partly compensates.

**NGFB is a credit play.** Its unsecured-heavy book makes credit its largest channel (`r bps(att("downside", "NGFB", "credit"))` in the downside, `r bps(att("upside", "NGFB", "credit"))` in the upside). And its receive-fixed hedge more than offsets its endowment: higher rates cost it `r ubps(att("downside", "NGFB", "pricing"))` through pricing in the downside, and lower rates add `r bps(att("upside", "NGFB", "pricing"))` in the upside. Over three years the downside costs NGFB `r rbn(st["baseline", "ni"] - st["downside", "ni"], 1)` of net income, while the unhedged sector's ROE actually rises.

**The variant shows how much rides on the SARB.** With the same contraction but rate cuts, the hedge earns NGFB `r bps(att("downside_cuts", "NGFB", "pricing"))` through pricing and its total loss is `r ubps(att("downside_cuts"))`, a little over half the stagflationary loss, while the unhedged sector loses `r ubps(att("downside_cuts", "Sector"))`. A structural hedge protects against the downturns of 2009 and 2020. It does not protect against a downturn that arrives with hikes.

NGFB's ROE sits below the sector's in every scenario, `r pct(st["baseline", "ngfb"])` against `r pct(st["baseline", "sector"])` in the baseline, because its unsecured book carries higher credit losses (`r pct(st["baseline", "clr"], 2)` of loans against `r pct(st["baseline", "sector_clr"], 2)`). The hedge narrows the gap: without it NGFB would earn `r pct(st["baseline", "ngfb_nohedge"])`. Its average fixed rate of `r num(N$hedge_fixed0, 2)`%, struck at actual swap rates over the past five years, sits above a floating leg averaging `r num(S$scen$float_mean, 2)`% over the horizon, and the carry grows from `r rbn(S$scen$hedge_carry[[1]], 1)` in the first year to `r rbn(S$scen$hedge_carry[[3]], 1)` in the third as the benchmark eases. That carry is not a free lunch. It is the value of a position taken when rates were higher, and it is what the hedge is paid for giving up the upside in a hiking cycle.

Capital and liquidity are not the binding constraint anywhere: CET1 never falls below `r pct(min(st$cet1_min))` against an 11.5% management floor, and the LCR never below `r pct(min(st$lcr_min), 0)`.

## How exposed are we?

The sensitivities answer the first ALCO question one variable at a time: each shock is held for the whole horizon around the baseline, and everything else stays put. As a conversion rate, one basis point of ROE is worth about `r rmn(bp_yr)` of net income a year.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity of NGFB's three-year average ROE to one-variable shocks around the baseline, with the hedge (teal) and without it (grey)."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-summary: "Figure: sensitivities"
shl <- c(repo_up_100 = "Repo +100 bps", repo_down_100 = "Repo -100 bps", gdp_down_1 = "GDP growth -1 pp",
         gov10y_up_100 = "10-year yield +100 bps", hpi_down_10 = "House prices -10%", cpi_up_1 = "CPI +1 pp",
         zar_weaker_10 = "Rand 10% weaker", unemp_up_2 = "Unemployment +2 pp")
sd2 <- data.frame(shock = factor(shl[se$shock], levels = rev(shl)), hedged = 1e4 * se$total, unhedged = 1e4 * snh[se$shock, "total"])
ggplot(sd2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = unhedged, xend = hedged, y = shock, yend = shock), colour = MUTE, linewidth = .5) +
  geom_point(aes(unhedged, shock, colour = "Without the hedge"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(hedged, shock, colour = "NGFB with its hedge"), size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(aes(hedged, shock, label = sprintf("%+.0f", hedged)), colour = FG, size = 3.1, vjust = -1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`NGFB with its hedge` = ACCENT, `Without the hedge` = MUTE), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Growth is the big exposure; the hedge turns rates into a small one",
       subtitle = "Change in three-year average ROE, bps", x = "bps of ROE", y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

* **Rates.** A repo path 100 bps higher costs hedged NGFB `r ubps(se["repo_up_100", "total"])` of ROE, and 100 bps lower adds `r ubps(se["repo_down_100", "total"])`. Without the hedge the same shocks would move it by `r bps(snh["repo_up_100", "total"])` and `r bps(snh["repo_down_100", "total"])`. The hedge was sized in Post 3 for deposits that reprice more slowly than the industry models now find, so it more than neutralises the endowment and leaves NGFB modestly liability-sensitive. That sounds like a technicality. It is the first hint that the hedge is a position rather than a hedge.
* **Growth.** One point less GDP growth for three years costs `r ubps(se["gdp_down_1", "total"])` (`r rbn(-se["gdp_down_1", "net_income"], 1)` of net income), `r ubps(se["gdp_down_1", "credit"])` of it through credit losses. This is NGFB's largest exposure by a distance.
* **The long bond, house prices, the rand and inflation.** A ten-year yield 100 bps higher costs `r ubps(se["gov10y_up_100", "total"])`, a 10% fall in house prices `r ubps(se["hpi_down_10", "total"])`, a rand 10% weaker `r ubps(se["zar_weaker_10", "total"])`. A point more inflation *adds* `r ubps(se["cpi_up_1", "total"])`, because fee income tracks nominal activity. It may be the only line on a bank's income statement that is pleased to see inflation.
* **Unemployment** barely registers (`r bps(se["unemp_up_2", "total"])`). Not because unemployment is harmless, but because no credit-loss relationship with unemployment survived testing once GDP was in it. The South African series moves too slowly, and too noisily, to identify a separate channel, so in this engine a labour-market shock shows up only through its GDP counterpart.

## Positioning before the scenario arrives

The other two ALCO questions are about action. The decision here is a set of balance-sheet moves made at the jump-off, each one unit in size: shift one percent of total assets out of HQLA into one of six lending books, replace one percent of wholesale funding with one of three kinds of deposit, or change the receive-fixed hedge by one percent of non-maturity deposits. The engine is the source of truth, and around the status quo it is close to linear in the moves. So for every scenario $s$ the gradient $G_s$, how much one unit of each move adds to three-year ROE, comes from re-running the engine with each move nudged half a unit up and half a unit down.

The naive thing is to maximise the engine's ROE, and it immediately embarrasses itself. Even with execution costs it grows every lending book out of HQLA, pushes `r nw(P$naive_up)` of the six to their upper bounds and claims `r ubps(P$naive_gain)` of probability-weighted ROE, the kind of number that wins a consultant a second engagement. The engine prices a new rand of lending at the book's *average* yield, loss rate and cost ratio, and holds equity fixed, so every risk asset looks better than HQLA. Whether NGFB should simply be bigger in cards is a franchise question (marginal pricing, cost to serve, adverse selection) that public data cannot answer. The positioning question is narrower and answerable: what should change *because* scenario X is coming?

So the status quo is taken to be optimal under the baseline, which is what a balance sheet built for the bank's central plan ought to be. That reveals an implied marginal cost for every move, $c = G_{\text{baseline}}$. If the plan is right at the margin, whatever one more unit of a move would add under the baseline must be exactly offset by costs the engine cannot see. It is the trick Black and Litterman used to back implied returns out of market weights [@BlackLitterman1992]. Instead of asking the model what the balance sheet should be, ask what the model must believe for the current balance sheet to be right, and trade only on departures from that. Positioning then trades on how a scenario *changes* each move's value:

$$\max_{x}\;\; \sum_s w_s\Big(R_s + (G_s - c)^{\top}x\Big) \;-\; \frac{\lambda}{2}\,\mathrm{Var}_w\big(R + Gx\big) \;-\; \sum_k \kappa_k\,x_k^2 .$$

$x$ is the vector of moves, $R_s$ the ROE in scenario $s$ if nothing moves, $w_s$ the scenario probabilities, and $(G_s - c)$ the extra value one unit of each move adds in scenario $s$ over and above the baseline. The middle term penalises spreading the outcomes across scenarios, with $\lambda$ setting how much; a bank that cares only about the average sets $\lambda = 0$. The last term is execution cost: pricing concessions and acquisition costs to grow a book within a year, attrition to shrink one. It is quadratic, so a two-unit move costs four times a one-unit move, which is roughly how franchises behave when you try to rush them. The moves are bounded, and the CET1 (11.5%) and LCR (120%) floors must hold.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-moves
#| code-summary: "Table: the moves"
mt <- data.frame(Move = mv$label, From = c(rep("HQLA", 6), rep("Wholesale funding", 3), "–"),
                 Unit = c(rep("1% of assets", 9), "1% of NMD"),
                 Bounds = sprintf("%+.1f to %+.1f", mv$lower, mv$upper),
                 `Execution cost of one unit` = ubps(mv$cost, 1),
                 `Worth under the baseline (implied cost)` = bps(cimp[mv$move], 1), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(mt, align = "lllrrr")
```

With one scenario treated as certain and nothing binding, the problem falls apart into one small problem per move, and each has a closed form. For move $k$, maximise $(G_{X,k} - c_k)\,x_k - \kappa_k x_k^2$. The benefit rises in a straight line, the cost in a parabola, and the best move is where one more unit adds exactly as much benefit as cost:

$$x_k^{*} \;=\; \frac{G_{X,k} - c_k}{2\,\kappa_k}, \qquad \text{net gain} \;=\; \sum_k \frac{(G_{X,k} - c_k)^2}{4\,\kappa_k} .$$

In words: move in the direction the scenario shifts the move's value, by an amount proportional to how far it shifts it, and inversely proportional to how expensive the move is to execute. Every result is then re-run through the full engine, which captures what the linear model misses (moves compound with growth, equity builds), and reported net of both the implied and the execution cost.

Take the hedge, because it does most of the work. Under the baseline one more point of hedge earns `r bps(h_c, 1)` of ROE, so that is its implied cost. Under the downside it earns `r bps(h_G, 1)`, because the floating leg it pays reprices up with the hikes. The net gradient is `r bps(h_G - h_c, 1)` a point and the execution cost `r ubps(h_k, 1)` per point squared, so the optimum is $`r sprintf("%.2f", 1e4 * (h_G - h_c))` / (2 \times `r sprintf("%.1f", 1e4 * h_k)`) = `r sprintf("%.1f", h_x)`$ points of non-maturity deposits, taking the hedge from `r pct(N$hedge_ratio)` to `r pct(N$hedge_ratio + h_x / 100)`.

The rest of the downside positioning follows the same logic. Deposits gain value in a hiking cycle, because their cost lags the policy rate, so `r pct((ps["downside", "fund_savings"] + ps["downside", "fund_operational"]) / 100, 2)` of assets of wholesale funding is swapped for savings and transactional deposits. Unsecured lending loses value as losses rise, so cards and personal loans are trimmed by `r pct(-(ps["downside", "into_cards"] + ps["downside", "into_personal"]) / 100, 2)` of assets. Nothing hits a bound or a floor. Positioned, NGFB's downside ROE improves by `r bps(gain["downside", "downside"])`, or `r srmn(gni["downside", "downside"])` of net income over three years. That recovers `r pct(gain["downside", "downside"] / -att("downside"), 0)` of the downside's `r ubps(att("downside"))` hit. Positioning cannot undo a credit cycle inside a year, and credit is what drives the downside.

Before the upside everything reverses: extend the hedge by `r sprintf("%.1f", ps["upside", "hedge"])` points to `r pct(N$hedge_ratio + ps["upside", "hedge"] / 100)`, since its floating leg now reprices down, let `r pct(-(ps["upside", "fund_savings"] + ps["upside", "fund_operational"]) / 100, 2)` of assets of deposits go, and grow cards and personal loans by `r pct((ps["upside", "into_cards"] + ps["upside", "into_personal"]) / 100, 2)` of assets. That earns `r bps(gain["upside", "upside"])` if the upside comes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-regret
#| fig-cap: "The cost of being wrong. Change in NGFB's three-year average ROE from positioning for the scenario in the row when the scenario in the column arrives, net of implied and execution costs, full engine."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| code-summary: "Figure: the regret matrix"
gm <- expand.grid(pos = rownames(gain), real = colnames(gain), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gm$v <- 1e4 * gain[cbind(gm$pos, gm$real)]
gm$pos <- factor(paste("Positioned for the", tolower(SC_LAB[gm$pos])), levels = rev(paste("Positioned for the", tolower(SC_LAB[c("baseline", "upside", "downside")]))))
gm$real <- factor(SC_LAB[gm$real], levels = SC_LAB[c("baseline", "upside", "downside")])
ggplot(gm, aes(real, pos, fill = v)) +
  geom_tile(colour = BG, linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(abs(v) < .05, "0", sprintf("%+.0f bps", v))), colour = FG, size = 4.2, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = WARN, mid = MID, high = ACCENT, midpoint = 0, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(title = "Being wrong costs more than being right earns", subtitle = "Scenario that arrives", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slate() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

Every positioning is a bet, and the honest way to present one is with its cost of being wrong alongside, not in an appendix in eight-point grey. Position for the downside and get the baseline instead, and it costs `r ubps(gain["downside", "baseline"])`. Get the upside instead, and it costs `r ubps(gain["downside", "upside"])`, or `r rbn(gni["downside", "upside"], 1)` of net income. The upside positioning costs `r ubps(gain["upside", "baseline"])` if the baseline arrives and `r ubps(gain["upside", "downside"])` if the downside does. So being wrong costs `r num(-gain["downside", "upside"] / gain["downside", "downside"], 1)` times what being right earns for the downside positioning, and `r num(-gain["upside", "downside"] / gain["upside", "upside"], 1)` times for the upside's. The two positionings are opposite bets on the same levers, which means a bigger bet on one scenario is automatically a bigger bet against the other.

The downside's single most important judgement is the SARB's response. Rerun the same contraction with 150 bps of cuts and the optimal hedge move flips sign, `r sprintf("%+.1f", P$cuts[["hedge"]])` points instead of `r sprintf("%+.1f", ps["downside", "hedge"])`, because the hedge becomes NGFB's protection rather than its cost. The credit leg does not flip: cards and personal loans are cut either way. The credit side of a downside positioning is robust to the policy response. The rate side is a bet on it.

What if there is no strong view? With the probabilities used here (`r pct(wts[["baseline"]], 0)` baseline, `r pct(wts[["upside"]], 0)` upside, `r pct(wts[["downside"]], 0)` downside) and a variance aversion of $\lambda = 4$, the probability-weighted positioning trims the hedge by `r sprintf("%.1f", -P$robust_x[["hedge"]])` points of non-maturity deposits and moves no other line by more than `r pct(ceiling(100 * max(abs(P$robust_x[names(P$robust_x) != "hedge"]))) / 1e4, 2)` of assets. The upside and the downside largely cancel, and when a bank genuinely does not know which is coming, the best response is close to the plan. The framework's value runs the other way. It tells the ALCO what to do, and what it costs if it is wrong, *as conviction about a scenario builds*. Positioning scales almost linearly with conviction until something binds.

Which leaves the question every ALCO eventually asks: what if we were braver? There are two different dials, and they behave differently. The first is to make bigger moves at the same cost. Scale the optimal move by a factor $\alpha$, and the benefit if the scenario arrives grows in proportion to $\alpha$ while the execution cost grows with its square:

$$\text{net gain}(\alpha) \;=\; \alpha\,(G - c)\,x^{*} \;-\; \kappa\,\alpha^2 x^{*2} \;=\; (2\alpha - \alpha^2)\,\frac{(G-c)^2}{4\kappa} .$$

The gain peaks at the optimum ($\alpha = 1$), is gone at twice the optimal size, and turns negative beyond. Meanwhile the loss if the scenario does *not* arrive keeps growing all the while, and faster than the gain ever did.

```{r}
#| label: fig-alpha
#| fig-cap: "Scaling the optimal downside positioning up and down at the same execution cost. The gain if the downside arrives follows the 2α − α² law until the hedge reaches its policy bound; the loss if it does not grows throughout."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-summary: "Figure: more aggressive?"
sz <- P$size; sz <- rbind(sz, data.frame(alpha = 0, realised = c("baseline", "upside", "downside"), gain = 0, gain_ni = 0, exp_gain = 0))
sz$who <- factor(SC_LAB[sz$realised], levels = names(SC_COL)[1:3])
ex <- unique(sz[, c("alpha", "exp_gain")])
law <- data.frame(alpha = seq(0, 3, .05)); law$v <- 1e4 * (2 * law$alpha - law$alpha^2) * gain["downside", "downside"]
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_line(data = law, aes(alpha, v), colour = WARN, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = .7) +
  geom_line(data = sz, aes(alpha, 1e4 * gain, colour = who), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = sz[sz$alpha > 0, ], aes(alpha, 1e4 * gain, colour = who), size = 2.4) +
  geom_line(data = ex, aes(alpha, 1e4 * exp_gain, colour = "Probability-weighted"), linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.45, y = 1e4 * (2 * 2.45 - 2.45^2) * gain["downside", "downside"] - 9, label = "2α − α² law", colour = FG, size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(SC_COL[1:3], `Probability-weighted` = FG), name = "If this arrives:") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "×")) +
  labs(title = "Doubling the bet wipes out the gain even when you are right",
       subtitle = "Net ROE gain from the downside positioning scaled by α, bps", x = "size of the moves, relative to the optimum", y = "bps of ROE") +
  theme_slate()
```

Doubling the optimal moves leaves nothing even if the downside arrives, and loses `r ubps(szp(2, "upside"))` if the upside does. The second dial is a bank that can execute more cheaply: one with a deposit franchise to spare, an underwriting machine ready to scale, or simply more time. The optimiser then chooses bigger moves. At a quarter of the execution cost the downside positioning makes `r bps(capq(.25, 1, "downside"))` if the downside comes, but loses `r ubps(capq(.25, 1, "upside"))` if the upside does. Either way, the loss if wrong grows faster than the gain if right. And with a `r pct(wts[["downside"]], 0)` chance of the downside, the probability-weighted value of full-conviction positioning is negative at every size. Positioning ahead of a downside is like packing an umbrella for a Highveld afternoon: cheap and sensible, and it will not stop the hail.

## Where NGFB should lean in

The positioning moved the balance sheet ahead of a scenario. Underneath it sits a commercial question: in which products, and in which phases of the cycle, does NGFB grow more slowly than its market and its peers, and is it worth fixing?

Two numbers place NGFB in each product and regime. The first is how fast the market grows in that regime, from the industry's history; no bank controls it. The second is NGFB's *share effect*, how much faster or slower than the market its book grows, from Stage 2. And because Stage 2 is a population, it also supplies a yardstick for the share effect: **par**, the typical large bank (the population mean); the **frontier**, a top-quintile large bank (the 80th percentile of the population's predictive distribution); and NGFB's percentile between them. Only population quantities are used, never an individual bank's estimate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-quadrant
#| fig-cap: "Market growth against NGFB's share effect, product by product and regime by regime. Bottom right is the uncomfortable corner: the market grows faster than usual and NGFB loses share. Grey cells need no action."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.8
#| code-summary: "Figure: where to lean in"
pq <- pb; pq$lab <- paste0(PROD_LAB[pq$product], ", ", pq$regime)
pq$act <- factor(pq$action, levels = c("Push", "Defend", "Guard", "Let go", "Ride", "Hold"))
act_col <- c(Push = ACCENT2, Defend = WARN, Guard = INDIGO, `Let go` = GREEN, Ride = ACCENT, Hold = MUTE)
nh <- pq[pq$action != "Hold", ]
ggplot(pq, aes(market_dev, ngfb_effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = act), size = ifelse(pq$action == "Hold", 2, 3.2), alpha = ifelse(pq$action == "Hold", .55, 1)) +
  (if (requireNamespace("ggrepel", quietly = TRUE))
     ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = nh, aes(label = lab), colour = FG, size = 2.9, seed = 20260622, box.padding = .45,
                              min.segment.length = .2, segment.colour = MUTE, segment.size = .3)
   else geom_text(data = nh, aes(label = lab), colour = FG, size = 2.9, vjust = -1, check_overlap = TRUE)) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.5, y = -6.6, label = "market grows, NGFB loses share", colour = MUTE, size = 3.1, hjust = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = act_col, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "NGFB under-participates when rates fall",
       subtitle = "Each point is a product in a regime. NGFB's share effect excludes its structural drift, so this is about the cycle.",
       x = "market growth in the regime, against its average (pp a year)", y = "NGFB's growth against the market (pp a year)") +
  theme_slate()
```

The rules that turn a cell into an action are economic, not statistical. **Push** where NGFB loses share in a regime when its market grows at or above its average: that is under-participation, the cheapest growth NGFB forgoes. **Defend** where it loses share in a weak market for a secured or funding product, because competitors are taking good-quality business, or loses deposit share in a growing deposit market, because that is funding it will later buy wholesale. **Guard** where it gains unsecured share while the market weakens: check that it isn't booking the business everybody else is declining. **Let go** where it cedes unsecured share in a contraction, which is risk appetite doing its job. **Ride** gains in a growing market, with capacity and pricing discipline.

The gap is in easing cycles. When rates fall, the card market grows `r num(pbc("cards", "easing", "market_growth"), 1)`% a year against an average of `r num(pbc("cards", "easing", "market_growth") - pbc("cards", "easing", "market_dev"), 1)`%, yet NGFB's card book grows `r num(-pbc("cards", "easing", "ngfb_effect"), 1)` points a year more slowly than the market (`r ord(pbc("cards", "easing", "percentile"))` percentile). It is not alone, since the typical large bank also loses `r num(-pbc("cards", "easing", "par"), 1)` points a year of card growth in an easing cycle, and the Challengers take `r pct(gnc("cards", "easing", "Challengers"), 0)` of what NGFB gives up. Corporate loans (`r sprintf("%+.1f", pbc("corp_all", "easing", "ngfb_effect"))` pp, `r ord(pbc("corp_all", "easing", "percentile"))` percentile) and vehicle and asset finance (`r sprintf("%+.1f", pbc("vaf", "easing", "ngfb_effect"))` pp, `r ord(pbc("vaf", "easing", "percentile"))` percentile) follow the same pattern. In hiking cycles it reverses, and NGFB gains card share (`r sprintf("%+.1f", pbc("cards", "hiking", "ngfb_effect"))` pp a year). The problem a bank might expect, losing cards when rates are high, is not NGFB's problem. Losing them when rates fall is.

Is it worth pushing? Share is worth buying only if the extra business earns more than it costs at the margin, and the scenario engine is the wrong tool for that, because it grows the whole bank along with the loan book. So each product's marginal economics are built up directly, per rand of balance:

$$\text{headroom} \;=\; r \;-\; f \;-\; \ell\,(f - r_{H}) \;-\; \text{EL} \;-\; \frac{k\,\rho\,\big(\text{CoE} - (1-\tau)\,f\big)}{1-\tau} .$$

A rand of new lending earns its rate $r$. It costs the marginal funding rate $f$, the funds-transfer price. It also costs the liquidity that funding needs: a quarter ($\ell = 25\%$) of a rand of wholesale funding must sit in HQLA earning $r_H$ rather than $f$. It loses its expected credit loss, EL. And it ties up capital: at a 12.5% CET1 target ($k$) and the product's risk weight $\rho$, that capital costs the 14.5% cost of equity less the after-tax funding it saves, and dividing by $1-\tau$ grosses the charge up to a pre-tax rate like everything else. What is left is the **headroom**: the most the business could cost to originate and service before it destroys value. The returns carry no costs by product, so this is the honest form of the answer. In the table below every column is in percent a year of the balance, and the headroom is the rate less the other four.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-margins
#| code-summary: "Table: marginal economics"
mp <- c("cards", "personal_other", "corp_all", "vaf", "mortgages_res", "mortgages_com")
mw <- mg[mg$funding == "wholesale", ]; rownames(mw) <- mw$product
mb <- mg[mg$funding == "blended", ]; rownames(mb) <- mb$product
knitr::kable(data.frame(Product = PROD_LAB[mp], `Rate (%)` = num(mw[mp, "rate"], 2), `FTP (%)` = num(mw[mp, "ftp"], 2),
                        `Liquidity` = num(mw[mp, "liquidity"], 2), `Expected loss` = num(mw[mp, "expected_loss"], 2),
                        `Capital charge` = num(mw[mp, "capital_charge"] / (1 - N$tax), 2),
                        `Headroom, wholesale funding (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", mw[mp, "headroom"]),
                        `Headroom, own deposits (pp)` = sprintf("%+.2f", mb[mp, "headroom"]), check.names = FALSE),
             align = "lrrrrrrr", row.names = FALSE)
```

Cards clear the bar comfortably even on wholesale funding (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mgc("cards", "wholesale"))` pp of headroom). Corporate lending clears it only narrowly (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mgc("corp_all", "wholesale"))` pp) and vehicle and asset finance barely at all (`r sprintf("%+.2f", mgc("vaf", "wholesale"))` pp), but funded with deposits both have `r num(mgc("corp_all", "blended"), 1)` and `r num(mgc("vaf", "blended"), 1)` pp to spare. The lesson is the same for every secured product: at NGFB's margins, lending growth pays when it brings its own funding.

The guard case is cards in a contraction. NGFB gains card share (`r sprintf("%+.1f", pbc("cards", "contraction", "ngfb_effect"))` pp a year, `r ord(pbc("cards", "contraction", "percentile"))` percentile) while the card market all but stops (`r num(pbc("cards", "contraction", "market_growth"), 1)`% a year). At the average card loss rate the extra book still pays, but in the downside its headroom on wholesale funding is only `r num(cards_guard, 1)` pp. If the accounts won in a downturn lose more than that above the average card loss rate, the share gain destroys value, and adverse selection makes that likely: in a contraction, the customer walking in is often the one other banks have just declined. The action is to tighten underwriting on new card business when GDP turns, not to celebrate the share.

## The tide and the swimming

The same split turns into a way of judging performance. A product's growth is the market's growth plus the bank's share effect. The first part is the macro environment, which no bank controls. The second is what management controls, and Stage 2 says what a typical large bank achieves in the same regimes. So a macro-adjusted target for product $p$ in quarter $t$ is

$$\text{target}_{p,t} \;=\; \underbrace{g^{\text{market}}_{p,t}}_{\text{realised, from the returns}} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{par}_p(\text{regime}_t)}_{\text{Stage 2}} \;+\; \text{ambition}_p ,$$

and performance is actual growth less the target. The market term is measured after the fact, so a bank is neither punished for a recession nor rewarded for a boom. The par term allows for what a typical large bank does in that phase of the cycle. The ambition is management's choice. Set in advance, the target becomes scenario-contingent. Looked back on, it separates the tide from the swimming. Warren Buffett's version is that you only find out who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out; a macro-adjusted target finds out while the tide is still in.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scorecards
#| fig-cap: "Macro-adjusted scorecards: NGFB's percentile among large banks for its share effect in each scenario (teal above par, red below), labelled with the share effect in pp a year."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| code-summary: "Figure: scorecards"
sk <- sc; sk$prod <- factor(PROD_LAB[sk$product], levels = PROD_LAB[c("mortgages_res", "mortgages_com", "vaf", "cards", "personal_other", "corp_all", "nmd", "beh_term")])
sk$scn <- factor(SC_LAB[sk$scenario], levels = rev(SC_LAB[c("baseline", "upside", "downside")]))
ggplot(sk, aes(prod, scn, fill = percentile)) +
  geom_tile(colour = BG, linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%\n%+.1f pp", 100 * percentile, share_effect)), colour = FG, size = 3.1, lineheight = .9) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = WARN, mid = MID, high = ACCENT, midpoint = .5, limits = c(0, 1), labels = percent, name = "percentile") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) vapply(x, function(z) paste(strwrap(z, 13), collapse = "\n"), "")) +
  labs(title = "Separating the tide from the swimming", subtitle = "NGFB's percentile among large banks, and its share effect", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slate() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8.5, lineheight = .9), legend.position = "right")
```

In the downside most of the slowdown in NGFB's books is the market's. Even so, NGFB is below par in home loans (`r ord(scc("downside", "mortgages_res"))` percentile), because a typical large bank gains mortgage share in a contraction as lenders retreat to secured credit, and NGFB gains less. Cards sit near the frontier (`r ord(scc("downside", "cards"))` percentile), which is exactly the guard case above, a reminder that a high percentile is not automatically good news. In the upside the growth is in cards, corporate lending and vehicle finance, and NGFB is below par in all three. The upside's message for management is to protect share where the growth is, not to bank the tide.

## Are the numbers right?

Every number in this post is computed inline and guarded: the render fails if a rebuild moves one far enough to change a sentence. That checks the arithmetic. It does not check the inputs the arithmetic takes on trust, and when I went looking, two of them were wrong.

### The hedge was priced off the wrong curve

Until free swap data turned up, the hedge's swap rates came from a proxy built inside the government curve:

$$s^{\text{proxy}}_{5} \;=\; \text{JIBAR} \;+\; 0.55\,\big(y^{\text{gov}}_{10} - \text{JIBAR}\big),$$

the three-month rate plus a fixed share of the ten-year bond's spread over it. It looks innocent and is not. Daily JIBAR swap fixings are now published by rbond.co.za [@Rbond2026], and against them the proxy fails in every quarter.

```{r}
#| label: fig-proxy
#| fig-cap: "The five-year JIBAR swap rate (quarterly average of daily fixings) against the proxy that priced the hedge, with three-month JIBAR and the five-year government yield. Source: rbond.co.za (CC BY 4.0), SARB, FRED."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-summary: "Figure: the swap proxy"
px <- rbind(data.frame(date = pr$date, v = pr$swap5y, s = "5-year swap (actual)"), data.frame(date = pr$date, v = pr$proxy, s = "Proxy inside the government curve"),
            data.frame(date = pr$date, v = pr$gov5y, s = "5-year government bond"), data.frame(date = pr$date, v = pr$jibar3m, s = "3-month JIBAR"))
px$s <- factor(px$s, levels = c("Proxy inside the government curve", "5-year government bond", "5-year swap (actual)", "3-month JIBAR"))
ggplot(px, aes(date, v, colour = s)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Proxy inside the government curve` = WARN, `5-year government bond` = ACCENT2,
                                 `5-year swap (actual)` = ACCENT, `3-month JIBAR` = MUTE), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(title = "The proxy overstated swap rates in every quarter",
       subtitle = sprintf("Proxy error %.1f to %.1f pp, %.1f pp on average", A$proxy_err[["min"]], A$proxy_err[["max"]], A$proxy_err[["mean"]]),
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

The proxy overstated the five-year swap rate by `r num(A$proxy_err[["min"]], 1)` to `r num(A$proxy_err[["max"]], 1)` percentage points, `r num(A$proxy_err[["mean"]], 1)` on average. The reason is structural rather than noise. South African government bonds pay a fiscal premium over swaps, the price of the tight link between the sovereign and the banks that hold its paper [@HesseMiyajima2022Nexus], and a curve built inside the bond curve inherits it. Pricing a swap off the bond curve is like pricing a Polo's insurance off a Range Rover's quote: same road, different risk. Priced off actual fixings, the hedge book's fixed rate falls from `r num(A$fixed0[["proxy"]], 2)`% to `r num(A$fixed0[["core"]], 2)`%, and NGFB's baseline ROE by `r ubps(corr["baseline", "d_roe"])` (`r rbn(corr["baseline", "ni_proxy"] - corr["baseline", "ni_v4"], 1)` of net income over three years). It was the largest single correction in this project, and it changed the story: before it, NGFB appeared to out-earn the sector, and that was mostly the proxy's excess carry, not the hedge.

### A broken equity series

Equity-price growth is a candidate driver in several of the industry models, standing in for household wealth and business confidence. The SARB all-share series that fed it had three level breaks that are not market moves: `r sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * eb$sarb[1])` in `r format(eb$date[1], "%B %Y")`, `r sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * eb$sarb[2])` in `r format(eb$date[2], "%B %Y")` and `r sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * eb$sarb[3])` in `r format(eb$date[3], "%B %Y")`, months in which the OECD's all-share index for South Africa moved `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * eb$oecd[1])`, `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * eb$oecd[2])` and `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * eb$oecd[3])`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-equity
#| fig-cap: "Annual growth of South African equity prices: the SARB all-share series the models used to see, and the OECD all-share index used now (FRED SPASTT01ZAM661N). The dotted lines mark the three level breaks."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| code-summary: "Figure: the broken equity series"
eq <- A$equity
el <- rbind(data.frame(date = eq$date, v = eq$eq_sarb, s = "SARB series (broken)"), data.frame(date = eq$date, v = eq$eq_oecd, s = "OECD index"))
ggplot(el, aes(date, v, colour = s)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = eb$date, colour = MUTE, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`SARB series (broken)` = WARN, `OECD index` = ACCENT), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = "Two crashes and a boom that never happened",
       subtitle = "Annual growth in equity prices, quarterly averages (log, %)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

In annual growth the breaks became gaps of up to sixty points. The models were seeing equity crashes of 40–55% through 2017–18 and 2021–22, and a 50% boom in 2023, none of which happened; anybody who held the JSE through 2023 would have noticed a 50% year. Equity growth now comes from the OECD index [@FRED2026SharePrices], the panel build stops if annual equity growth ever exceeds 45% again, and every model was re-estimated on the clean series. Data checks are unglamorous. They are also the only part of a modelling project that the models themselves cannot do.

### How rate-sensitive is NGFB, really?

Banks publish the effect of a parallel 100 bp move on their next twelve months' net interest income, which gives a yardstick. The engine's equivalent moves every rate by 100 bps on the static balance sheet, with deposit costs and loan spreads following their projected pass-through. Unhedged, NGFB is asset-sensitive like the sector (`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * ns["unhedged", "up_pct"])` of NII against the sector's `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * ns["sector", "up_pct"])`), and more so than one large South African bank's 2025 disclosure (`r pct(A$disclosure[["sens_bn"]] / A$disclosure[["nii_bn"]])`). With its hedge, NGFB is *liability*-sensitive (`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * ns["hedged", "up_pct"])`), which is not what large South African banks report. The published bank hedges about R`r num(A$disclosure[["hedge_bn"]], 0)`bn of its endowment; NGFB hedges `r rbn(N$hedge_notional)`.

The canonical hedge ratio was sized in the deposit posts for slower deposit repricing than the industry models now find. With faster repricing, the ratio at which a 100 bp move leaves first-year NII unchanged falls to `r pct(A$neutral_ratio, 0)` of non-maturity deposits. By that yardstick NGFB is over-hedged: belt, braces and a second belt. File that away; it comes back.

### JIBAR's end

The engine prices ten quarters beyond JIBAR, so the transition is modelled rather than assumed away. The SARB's Market Practitioners Group set the timetable in December 2025 [@SARB2025JIBARCessation]: no new JIBAR-linked contracts from 1 May 2026; cleared JIBAR swaps converted by the clearing houses into ZARONIA overnight-index swaps in late November 2026, keeping their fixed rates, with the floating leg paying compounded ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp [@CME2026Zaronia; @SARB2023Conventions]; and the last JIBAR fixing on 31 December 2026, after which contracts that still reference it fall back to compounded ZARONIA plus the same credit adjustment spread.

That spread, the CAS, is the five-year median of three-month JIBAR less compounded ZARONIA. Over the 36 months of daily data the basis averaged `r num(mean(jz$basis) / 100, 2)` pp, between `r num(min(jz$basis) / 100, 2)` and `r num(max(jz$basis) / 100, 2)` pp as monthly averages.

```{r}
#| label: fig-basis
#| fig-cap: "Three-month JIBAR less ZARONIA, monthly averages of daily fixings, against the fixed fallback spread of 16.19 bp. Source: rbond.co.za (CC BY 4.0), SARB Market Practitioners Group."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4
#| code-summary: "Figure: the JIBAR-ZARONIA basis"
ggplot(jz, aes(date, basis)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100 * tr$spreads[["cas"]], colour = ACCENT2, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = ACCENT, linewidth = 1) + geom_point(colour = ACCENT, size = 1.6) +
  annotate("text", x = min(jz$date), y = 100 * tr$spreads[["cas"]] + 1.2, label = "fallback spread: 16.19 bp", colour = FG, size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 30)) +
  labs(title = "The fallback spread sits at the basis it replaces",
       subtitle = "3-month JIBAR less ZARONIA, bp", x = NULL, y = "bp") +
  theme_slate()
```

Because the CAS is the long-run median of the basis it replaces, the switch is level-neutral by design: against a run that keeps JIBAR going to 2029, NGFB's baseline ROE moves by `r bps(tsw["baseline", "d_roe"], 1)`. What changes is risk, in three ways.

* **The basis stops floating.** A three-month term rate carries the market's expected policy move over the coming quarter and the banks' own term and credit premium. ZARONIA compounded in arrears carries neither, and the CAS is fixed. NGFB pays the benchmark on net (`r rbn(tr$exposure[["assets"]])` of floating assets against `r rbn(tr$exposure[["funding"]])` of floating funding and a hedge notional of `r rbn(tr$exposure[["hedge"]])`), so each 10 bp widening of the basis used to cost it about `r rmn(-tr$exposure[["net"]] * 0.001)` of annual NII, and from 2027 costs nothing. Funding stress does not disappear. It moves into the spreads at which banks issue paper over the overnight rate.
* **The spread is at risk on the asset side.** Converted and fallback contracts keep the 16.19 bp, but loans re-papered onto ZARONIA are priced in negotiation, and a borrower quoted "ZARONIA plus the old margin" has quietly pocketed the CAS, and will be telling the story at year-end functions for years. If NGFB lost it on every floating-rate asset from 2027, its ROE would fall by `r ubps(cas$d_roe[cas$scenario == "baseline" & cas$case == "assets"])`. Pricing new ZARONIA business at all-in parity is worth exactly that.
* **The hedge is unaffected.** The clearing houses keep each swap's fixed rate and pay ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp on the floating leg, so the book's carry does not change.

One more check, on a channel the engine does not have. A recession could widen bank funding spreads beyond anything the benchmark captures, and once the benchmark is an overnight rate, that is the only place funding stress can show up. I regressed the sector's NCD spread over JIBAR on its own lag and the repo change, adding GDP growth, unemployment, a contraction kink, the curve's slope and the ten-year yield one at a time. None is significant. What moves the measured spread is mechanical: when the SARB cuts, the average cost of the NCD book lags JIBAR down and the spread widens for a few quarters. The one genuine funding shock in the sample, the global squeeze of late 2008, arrived before South Africa's GDP turned. Funding stress keeps its own diary. So a funding shock is a stress overlay, not a scenario relationship: 100 bps on wholesale funding and NCDs costs NGFB `r ubps(fo["baseline", "d_roe"])` of ROE.

## More levers, and a map of what drives them

The positioning moved the balance sheet's mix. An ALCO has more levers than that, and most of them are rate, spread, liquidity and capital decisions that a macro view should drive directly. Each one below is run through the full engine in every scenario, against NGFB's plan, in the order an ALCO sets them.

| Lever | The decision | The premium it earns | Its macro signal | The risk it takes, and where it shows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hedge ratio | share of non-maturity deposits received fixed | fixed over floating: a view on the policy path | the policy rate against neutral (R1) | rates rise: NII and EVE |
| Reinvestment tenor | tenor at which maturing swaps are replaced | the swap curve's term premium | the policy rate against neutral (R2) | today's rates locked in for longer: EVE |
| Ten-year bonds in HQLA | share of the buffer held in ten-year government bonds | the term premium and the fiscal premium | the curve's slope (R3) | the long bond sells off: OCI, CET1, EVE |
| Asset-swapped bonds | share held in five-year bonds swapped to floating | the fiscal premium alone | the bond–swap spread (R6) | the spread widens: OCI and CET1 |
| Size of the buffer | Treasury bills released to repay wholesale funding | wholesale funding's cost over the bills' yield | stress: GDP or the rand (R7) | less liquidity going into a stress: LCR, NSFR |
| Payout | share of profit paid out | equity returned: a smaller ROE denominator | growth and capital (R4) | a thinner cushion into a downturn: CET1 |
| Unsecured growth | card and personal-loan growth | volume and margin | the labour market (R5) | credit losses |

Read down, the map is the order of an ALCO's decisions: first how much of the deposit franchise's rate sensitivity to convert to fixed, then how to hold the liquidity regulation requires and how much of it to hold, then how much capital to keep. Read across, it says why each lever has its own macro signal. Each earns a different premium, and a premium is worth collecting when it is large. It also says why the levers must be chosen under limits, because every setting that earns more takes a risk the three-year ROE does not price, and the risks land in different places. The R-numbers are the macro-keyed rules tested in the lab further down.

```{r}
#| label: fig-levers
#| fig-cap: "Each lever's effect on NGFB's three-year average ROE in each scenario, against the plan. Rate views fan out across the scenarios; the term-premium and spread levers pay in all of them."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| code-summary: "Figure: the levers in the scenarios"
sel <- rbind(c("Hedge ratio", "80%", "Hedge ratio at 80%"), c("Hedge ratio", "0%", "Hedge ratio at 0%"),
             c("Reinvestment tenor", "10 years", "Reinvest at 10 years"), c("Reinvestment tenor", "7 years", "Reinvest at 7 years"),
             c("HQLA duration", "A quarter of HQLA in 10-year bonds", "A quarter of HQLA in 10-year bonds"),
             c("Asset swap", "A quarter of HQLA in asset-swapped 5-year bonds", "A quarter of HQLA asset-swapped"),
             c("Liquidity buffer", "LCR 160% at the jump-off", "Buffer cut to an LCR of 160%"),
             c("Payout", "70% of earnings", "Payout at 70%"),
             c("Distribution", "Capital above a 12.5% CET1 returned at the jump-off", "Capital above 12.5% CET1 returned"),
             c("Deposit pricing", "10% less of rises, 10% more of cuts", "Deposit pricing (upper bound)"))
ll <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(sel)), function(i) {
  r <- lvs[lvs$lever == sel[i, 1] & lvs$setting == sel[i, 2], ]
  data.frame(lab = sel[i, 3], scn = names(SC_COL), v = 1e4 * c(r$d_roe_baseline, r$d_roe_upside, r$d_roe_downside, r$d_roe_cuts),
             w = 1e4 * r$d_roe_weighted) }))
ll$lab <- factor(ll$lab, levels = rev(sel[, 3])); ll$scn <- factor(ll$scn, levels = names(SC_COL))
rng <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(ll, ll$lab), function(d) data.frame(lab = d$lab[1], lo = min(d$v), hi = max(d$v), w = d$w[1])))
ggplot() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_segment(data = rng, aes(x = lo, xend = hi, y = lab, yend = lab), colour = MUTE, linewidth = 1.6, alpha = .5) +
  geom_point(data = ll, aes(v, lab, colour = scn), size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = rng, aes(w, lab), shape = 23, size = 3.4, fill = FG, colour = BG) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = SC_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Rate views fan out; premia pay everywhere",
       subtitle = "Change in three-year average ROE against the plan, bps. Diamond: probability-weighted.",
       x = "bps of ROE", y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

### The hedge ratio is a rate view

```{r}
#| label: fig-ratio
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's three-year average ROE against the structural hedge ratio. Changes are made at the jump-off with five-year swaps; the existing book's locked-in carry stays either way. Dotted: the plan's ratio and the rate-neutral ratio."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-summary: "Figure: the hedge ratio"
rl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("baseline", "upside", "downside", "cuts"), function(k)
  data.frame(ratio = rc$ratio, v = rc[[k]], scn = SC_LAB[[if (k == "cuts") "downside_cuts" else k]])))
rl$scn <- factor(rl$scn, levels = names(SC_COL))
ggplot(rl, aes(ratio, v, colour = scn)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(N$hedge_ratio, A$neutral_ratio), colour = MUTE, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = A$neutral_ratio, y = .171, label = "rate-neutral", colour = FG, size = 3.1, hjust = 1.08) +
```
