```{r}
  annotate("text", x = N$hedge_ratio, y = .171, label = "plan", colour = FG, size = 3.1, hjust = -.15) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = SC_COL, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "A straight line in every scenario: the best hedge ratio is a corner",
       subtitle = "Three-year average ROE against the share of non-maturity deposits received fixed",
       x = "hedge ratio (share of non-maturity deposits)", y = "ROE") +
  theme_slate()
```

A receive-fixed swap earns its fixed rate and pays the floating benchmark. So more hedge pays in every scenario in which the benchmark falls below the rate the swap was struck at, and costs in every scenario in which it rises above. ROE is therefore a straight line in the hedge ratio, and the best ratio is always a corner: as much hedge as policy allows if your view is the baseline, the upside or a downturn with cuts, and none at all if your view is the stagflationary downside. Each ten points of non-maturity deposits received fixed adds `r ubps(slope10("baseline"))` of ROE in the baseline and costs `r ubps(slope10("downside"))` in the downside. At the scenario weights more hedge wins, because the five-year swap at the jump-off (`r num(LV$swap5_jo, 2)`%) priced the SARB's 2026 increases but not the baseline's later cuts. That is the bank's rate view against the market's, and it should be sized as a bet. The structural answer is the rate-neutral `r pct(A$neutral_ratio, 0)`, where earnings move least with a parallel shift.

### Reinvestment tenor: the term premium

One twentieth of the hedge matures every quarter, so within three years three-fifths of the book is reinvested. Reinvest at ten years instead of five and each tranche earns the swap curve's term premium, about `r num(A$spreads$spread[A$spreads$tenor == 10] - A$spreads$spread[A$spreads$tenor == 5], 1)` point a year more over 2023–2026, which is worth `r bps(lv("Reinvestment tenor", "10 years"))` of ROE in every scenario alike. It is not free. The book's PV01, the change in its value for a one basis point move in rates, rises by `r pct(LV$pv01$vs_plan[LV$pv01$tenor_q == 40], 0)`, so the economic value of equity becomes more sensitive to rates, the interest-rate-risk limits [@BCBS2016IRRBB] bind sooner, and today's rates are locked in for longer. Seven years is the halfway house (`r bps(lv("Reinvestment tenor", "7 years"))`, `r sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * LV$pv01$vs_plan[LV$pv01$tenor_q == 28])` PV01).

### Ten-year bonds in the buffer: the term and fiscal premia

NGFB's liquidity buffer sits in Treasury bills and cash. Level 1 government bonds count the same towards the LCR [@BCBS2013LCR], and South Africa's curve pays about two points for the duration: the ten-year bond yielded `r num(LV$gov10_jo, 2)`% in the jump-off quarter against `r num(asj$float3m, 2)`% for three-month JIBAR. Moving a quarter of the buffer into ten-year bonds adds `r bps(lv("HQLA duration", "A quarter of HQLA in 10-year bonds"))` of probability-weighted ROE, most where the long yield falls (`r bps(hq["downside_cuts", "d_roe"])` in a downturn with cuts) and least in the stagflationary downside (`r bps(hq["downside", "d_roe"])`).

The price shows up somewhere the ROE does not look, and it needs a word on accounting. Banks usually hold their liquidity bonds at fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) under IFRS 9 [@IFRS9]. The coupon runs through net interest income like any other asset's. The price change does not touch profit while the bond is held: it sits in the OCI reserve inside equity, and that reserve counts in CET1. Sell the bond and the accumulated gain or loss is recycled from the reserve into profit. And because Level 1 assets count in the LCR at market value, a price fall shrinks the buffer too. So a long bond in the buffer earns its carry in the income statement and takes its price risk in capital and liquidity, like a lodger who pays the rent on time and now and then floods the bathroom. At the downside's peak the mark-to-market costs `r ubps(hq["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"])` of CET1, and a sovereign shock larger than the scenario's (2015 and 2020 both moved the long bond by more) would cost more.

### Asset-swapped bonds: the fiscal premium without the duration

A ten-year bond held for liquidity earns two premia over bills. The *term premium* is the reward for interest-rate risk. The *fiscal premium* is what South African government bonds pay over the swap curve, the reward for sovereign and supply risk. An asset swap separates them. Buy a five-year government bond yielding $y^{\text{bond}}_5$ and, against it, pay fixed on a five-year swap at $s_5$ while receiving the floating benchmark $f_t$. The bond's coupon goes out through the swap's fixed leg and the benchmark comes back through its floating leg, so what is left is a floating-rate asset paying the benchmark plus the *bond–swap spread*, $bs = y^{\text{bond}}_5 - s_5$. Against the Treasury bill it replaces, each rand earns

$$\text{carry} \;=\; \underbrace{y^{\text{bond}}_{5} - s_{5}}_{\text{bond–swap spread, locked in at purchase}} \;+\; \underbrace{f_t - y^{\text{bill}}_t}_{\text{the bills' discount to the benchmark}} .$$

In the jump-off quarter the five-year bond yielded `r num(asj$gov5y, 2)`% against a five-year swap of `r num(LV$swap5_jo, 2)`%, a spread of `r num(asj$bs, 2)` pp, and bills yield about 0.15 pp under the benchmark. That is a pickup of roughly 0.8 pp a year, and none of it depends on where the policy rate goes.

It does depend on the spread, and a scenario says nothing directly about the spread: it carries the ten-year yield and the floating benchmark, not a swap curve that prices the policy path. So the spread is modelled, from one piece of economic logic. Both curves price the expected path of the policy rate, so a policy-driven move should leave their difference alone. What is left of a move in the long bond once the policy part is stripped out is the fiscal premium and global yields, and the spread should absorb some share of that:

$$\Delta bs_t \;=\; \kappa\,\Big[\,\Delta y^{\text{gov}}_{10,t} \;-\; \beta\,\Delta f_t\,\Big] .$$

$\beta$ is how far the ten-year yield moves for each point of the floating benchmark. It is only `r num(bsm$beta, 2)` (three-year changes since 2005, $t$ = `r num(bsm$beta_t, 1)`): the long end barely follows the policy rate. $\kappa$ is the share of the *remaining* move that lands on the bond–swap spread, `r num(bsm$kappa, 2)`, estimated on monthly levels since late 2023 ($t$ = `r num(bsm$kappa_t, 1)`, $R^2$ = `r num(bsm$kappa_r2, 2)`). About a quarter of a fiscal or global sell-off in the long bond shows up in the spread, and the swap curve moves with the rest. Month-on-month changes give a smaller `r num(bsm$kappa_d1, 2)`, short-run noise that does not accumulate; for a book held for years, the level relationship is the relevant one, and the larger number is also the more prudent. The model does miss the most recent months, when swap rates rose faster than bond yields as the market began to price the SARB's hikes and the spread compressed further than the long bond's level implies.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spread
#| fig-cap: "The five-year bond–swap spread, monthly, against the model's fit: a share κ of the ten-year yield's move net of β times the benchmark's. The spread compressed by more than half as the long bond rallied."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| code-summary: "Figure: the bond-swap spread"
bf <- bsm$fit
bl <- rbind(data.frame(date = bf$date, v = bf$bs5, s = "5-year bond–swap spread"), data.frame(date = bf$date, v = bf$fitted, s = "Model"))
ggplot(bl, aes(date, v, colour = s, linetype = s)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`5-year bond–swap spread` = ACCENT, Model = ACCENT2), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`5-year bond–swap spread` = "solid", Model = "22"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.8)) +
  labs(title = "The fiscal premium, priced monthly",
       subtitle = sprintf("pp. Mean %.2f since late 2023; %.2f at the jump-off.", bsm$bs_mean, asj$bs), x = NULL, y = "pp") +
  theme_slate()
```

What the asset swap does to the risk measures is the reason it matters later. **Economic value of equity: nothing.** The swap carries the bond's interest-rate sensitivity away, so the position uses none of the EVE budget. **Spread: everything.** What is left is credit-spread risk in the banking book. If the fiscal premium widens, the bond falls against the swap; with the bond at FVOCI and the swap designated as a hedge of its rate risk, the rate parts offset and the spread part sits in the OCI reserve, and so in CET1. The book's spread PV01 is R`r num(LV$as_spv01 / 1e3, 1)`m per basis point, so a 100 bp widening at the jump-off, about `r nw(round(1 / widen_max))` times the largest rise since the swap data begin, would cost `r ubps(LV$as_shock100)` of CET1 after tax. **Liquidity: a little.** A government bond is Level 1 like a bill, so buying it does not move the LCR, but a spread widening lowers the buffer's market value. A rate-driven price fall does not, because the cleared swap pays it back daily as variation margin.

A quarter of the buffer (`r rbn(LV$theta * LV$H0)`) in asset-swapped bonds adds `r ubps(min(asw$d_roe))` to `r ubps(max(asw$d_roe))` of ROE in every scenario, because its income does not care about the policy path. The stagflationary downside's sovereign stress widens the spread to `r num(asw["downside", "spread_max"], 2)` pp at its worst, which costs `r ubps(asw["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"])` of CET1 through OCI, about a seventh of the ten-year book's `r ubps(hq["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"])`, for 40% of its return. The ten-year book earns more because it also collects the term premium, and the term premium is paid for interest-rate risk that the asset swap does not take. It is the closest thing in this post to a free lunch, and like every free lunch in Sandton, somebody else is paying: here, the sovereign.

### The size of the buffer: what surplus liquidity costs

NGFB's LCR starts at `r pct(LV$lcr0, 0)`, against the `r pct(N$lcr_sector, 0)` the sector publishes and the 120% NGFB sets as its own floor. The surplus sits in Treasury bills, and at the margin it is funded with wholesale funding, so every rand of it earns the bill rate and costs the wholesale rate. That negative carry averages `r num(LV$buf_spread, 2)` pp a year over the baseline, about `r rmn(LV$buf_spread / 100 * 1e6)` before tax for each R1bn. Release bills and repay wholesale funding with them, and the saving is roughly nine basis points of ROE per R10bn, the same in every scenario, because it is a spread rather than a rate view. Cutting the LCR to 160% releases `r rbn(bufs("LCR 160% at the jump-off", "release"))` and adds `r bps(bufs("LCR 160% at the jump-off"))`. The lowest LCR across the scenarios is then `r pct(min(buf$lcr_min[buf$setting == "LCR 160% at the jump-off"]), 0)` and the lowest NSFR `r pct(min(buf$nsfr_min[buf$setting == "LCR 160% at the jump-off"]), 0)`, both far above their floors. What stops the release is not a ratio but the wholesale book itself. At 160% NGFB has repaid `r pct(bufs("LCR 160% at the jump-off", "release") / LV$wholesale_line$balance, 0)` of its wholesale funding, and releasing more would leave the bills with nothing dear to repay.

Surplus liquidity is the generator in the garage: you pay for it every month and resent it until the evening you need it. The engine does not stress run-offs, funding spreads or fire-sale prices, so it sees what the surplus costs but not what it buys. An LCR of 160% is still above the roughly 150% the sector holds, which the previous post found to be about the right size for a run on a quarter of the money that can actually leave. Even so, the release is a size decision for the bank's own liquidity stress test, not for the LCR alone.

### Capital and deposit pricing

The last two levers are quicker. NGFB starts with a CET1 ratio of `r pct(N$cet1_0)` and builds capital at a 50% payout. A 70% payout adds `r bps(lv("Payout", "70% of earnings"))` of probability-weighted ROE with the CET1 trough at `r pct(lv("Payout", "70% of earnings", "cet1_min"))`, close to the 11.5% floor, and returning the `r rbn(LV$excess, 1)` above a 12.5% target at the jump-off adds `r bps(lv("Distribution", "Capital above a 12.5% CET1 returned at the jump-off"))`. Payout is the natural macro-contingent lever: more in the upside, less going into a downturn, on the same principle as not booking Mauritius until the bonus has cleared. Passing 10% less of each policy-rate rise and 10% more of each cut to non-maturity deposit rates adds `r bps(lv("Deposit pricing", "10% less of rises, 10% more of cuts"))`, but that is an upper bound, because nothing in the engine prices the deposits it would lose.

Together, ten-year reinvestment, a quarter of HQLA in ten-year bonds and the capital distribution add `r bps(lv("Combined", "Ten-year reinvestment, HQLA duration and the distribution"))` at the scenario weights, and CET1 stays above the floor in every scenario, with a trough of `r pct(min(combo$cet1_min))`. Unless, that is, the bonds are marked through OCI, in which case the downside's peak takes CET1 to `r pct(combo["downside", "cet1_min_fvoci"])`, below the 11.5% floor. Three levers that each look fine on their own do not fit together, and the reason shows up where the ROE does not look. Hold that thought too.

## The strategy lab: sixty-one histories

The scenarios ask *what if X happens*. A positioning decision also has to survive what nobody wrote down, and the most honest set of those outcomes a South African bank has is its own history. The lab replays every complete twelve-quarter macro episode since 2008, `r RB$n_episodes` overlapping windows from `r info$episode[1]` to `r info$episode[nrow(info)]`, from today's starting point, and runs each through the whole chain: industry models, NGFB's share dynamics, the engine. Rates, the long bond, inflation and unemployment move by the change they made in the episode. GDP, house prices, the rand and equities grow as they grew, compounded from today's levels, which stops an episode that starts in the base-effect quarters of 2020–21 from shifting its whole path.

This is historical simulation, the market-risk workhorse, applied to a balance sheet. No distribution is assumed, but only history's episodes can occur, consecutive windows share eleven of their twelve quarters, and the sample holds exactly one global financial crisis and one pandemic, which is two more than anybody wanted and still not many.

```{r}
#| label: fig-episodes
#| fig-cap: "The replayed macro histories (grey: each a twelve-quarter window of South African history since 2008, applied to today's starting point) and the scenarios (colour)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| code-summary: "Figure: sixty-one histories"
ep <- L$paths
epl <- rbind(data.frame(path = ep$path, kind = ep$kind, date = ep$date, v = ep$repo, var = "Repo rate (%)"),
             data.frame(path = ep$path, kind = ep$kind, date = ep$date, v = ep$gdp_yy, var = "Real GDP growth, y/y (%)"))
epl$var <- factor(epl$var, levels = c("Repo rate (%)", "Real GDP growth, y/y (%)"))
ens <- epl[epl$kind == "episode", ]; scl <- epl[epl$kind != "episode", ]
scl$scn <- factor(SC_LAB[scl$path], levels = names(SC_COL))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = ens, aes(date, v, group = path), colour = MUTE, alpha = .35, linewidth = .45) +
  geom_line(data = scl, aes(date, v, colour = scn), linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~var, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = SC_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "History is a much wider fan than three scenarios",
       subtitle = sprintf("%d episodes replayed from the 2026Q2 jump-off", RB$n_episodes), x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

The episodes span far more than the scenarios do. The policy rate averages anywhere from `r num(-min(pl$d_repo_mean), 1)` points below today's to `r num(max(pl$d_repo_mean), 1)` above (`r n_up` episodes with higher rates on average, `r n_dn` with lower, the rest broadly flat), average real GDP growth runs from `r num(min(info$gdp_mean), 1)`% to `r num(max(info$gdp_mean), 1)`%, and the deepest quarter is the pandemic's `r num(min(info$gdp_min), 1)`%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-planhist
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's plan across the histories: three-year average ROE against the episode's average policy rate relative to today, coloured by average real GDP growth. Dotted: the 14.5% cost of equity."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| code-summary: "Figure: the plan across the histories"
ggplot(pl, aes(d_repo_mean, roe, colour = gdp_mean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = M$coe, colour = MUTE, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = max(pl$d_repo_mean), y = M$coe, label = "cost of equity", colour = FG, size = 3.1, hjust = 1, vjust = -.6) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#1c4a52", high = "#8fe3ee", name = "average GDP growth (%)") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "The plan earns its cost of equity in one history out of sixty-one",
       subtitle = sprintf("Average %.1f%%, 5th percentile %.1f%%. Growth and the rate path explain %.0f%% of the spread.",
                          100 * plan_roe, 100 * plan_p5, 100 * L$drivers_r2),
       x = "average repo rate over the episode, against today (pp)", y = "three-year average ROE") +
  theme_slate() + theme(legend.key.width = unit(1.4, "cm"))
```

NGFB's plan averages `r pct(plan_roe)` across the histories, between `r pct(min(pl$roe))` (`r pl$path[which.min(pl$roe)]`, through the pandemic) and `r pct(max(pl$roe))` (`r pl$path[which.max(pl$roe)]`, the rebound from it), with a 5th percentile of `r pct(plan_p5)`. It earns the 14.5% cost of equity in `r nw(round(ld["Plan", "coe_hit"] * RB$n_episodes))` of the `r RB$n_episodes`. Two macro numbers explain almost all of that spread. A regression across the episodes,

$$\overline{\text{ROE}}_e \;\approx\; a \;+\; b_{\text{gdp}}\,\bar g_e \;+\; b_{\text{repo}}\,\overline{\Delta r}_e ,$$

finds each point of average GDP growth $\bar g_e$ worth `r bps(drv[["gdp_mean"]])` of ROE and each point by which the policy rate averages above today's, $\overline{\Delta r}_e$, worth `r bps(drv[["d_repo_mean"]])`: that is the liability sensitivity the hedge gives NGFB. Together they explain `r pct(L$drivers_r2, 0)` of the variation. The regression is descriptive; overlapping windows make its precision look better than it is.

Each strategy is judged the way an ALCO would judge it: its average ROE across the episodes, its bad case (the 5th percentile), how often it beats the plan, and two risks the three-year ROE does not price. The first is the CET1 trough with any bonds at fair value, so that the OCI reserve counts. The second is interest-rate risk, measured the way the IRRBB outlier test measures it [@BCBS2016IRRBB], as the change in the economic value of the hedge and bond books for a 200 bp rise:

$$\frac{\Delta \text{EVE}}{\text{CET1}} \;=\; \frac{200 \times \text{PV01}}{\text{CET1}} ,$$

where PV01 is the change in the books' value for a one basis point parallel move.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hedgefrontier
#| fig-cap: "Static hedge positioning across the histories: average ROE against its spread (standard deviation across the episodes), for each hedge ratio (labels) and reinvestment tenor (colour). The plan is ringed."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-summary: "Figure: the static hedge frontier"
fh <- fr; fh$ten <- factor(paste(fh$tenor, "years"), levels = paste(c(3, 5, 7, 10), "years"))
fh$lab <- ifelse(fh$tenor == 10, paste0(round(100 * fh$ratio), "%"), "")
ggplot(fh, aes(100 * roe_sd, roe_mean)) +
  geom_path(aes(group = ten, colour = ten), linewidth = .7, data = fh[order(fh$ten, fh$ratio), ]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = ten), size = 2.8) +
  geom_point(data = fh[abs(fh$ratio - .5) < 1e-3 & fh$tenor == 5, ], shape = 21, size = 7, colour = FG, stroke = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab), colour = FG, size = 3.1, hjust = -.45) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`3 years` = MUTE, `5 years` = ACCENT, `7 years` = INDIGO, `10 years` = ACCENT2), name = "reinvestment tenor") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Earnings vary least near the rate-neutral ratio; ten years pays at every ratio",
       subtitle = "Each line runs from a 0% to an 80% hedge ratio", x = "spread of ROE across the histories (pp)", y = "average ROE") +
  theme_slate()
```

Three things stand out from the static hedge settings. **Earnings vary least near the rate-neutral ratio:** the spread across the histories is smallest at `r pct(A$neutral_ratio, 0)` reinvested at ten years (`r num(100 * frc(.37, 10, "roe_sd"), 2)` pp, against the plan's `r num(100 * frc(.5, 5, "roe_sd"), 2)`), because with more receive-fixed the hedge dominates and with less the endowment does. **Longer reinvestment pays at every ratio, whichever way rates go:** at the plan's ratio, ten years instead of five adds `r bps(ld["50% at 10 years", "d_roe_mean"])` on average and beats the plan in every episode, `r bps(ld["50% at 10 years", "d_roe_up"])` when rates rise and `r bps(ld["50% at 10 years", "d_roe_down"])` when they fall. Its cost is outside the ROE: a 200 bp rise would take a further `r pct(ld["50% at 10 years", "d_eve200"])` of CET1 off the books' value. **More hedge is a rate view:** receiving fixed on 80% of deposits at five years adds `r bps(ld["80% at 5 years", "d_roe_mean"])` on average, but `r bps(ld["80% at 5 years", "d_roe_up"])` when rates rise and `r bps(ld["80% at 5 years", "d_roe_down"])` when they fall, with a 5th percentile of `r bps(ld["80% at 5 years", "d_roe_p5"])`.

### Rules that read the macro picture

Static settings are chosen today and left alone. The lab's other question is whether settings that *respond* to the macro picture do better. Seven rules, one per lever, each reading only what was known at the end of the previous quarter:

| Rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| R1 hedge ratio | the plan's ratio plus 10 points of deposits for each point the policy rate stood above its 6.25% neutral level, within 20–80% |
| R2 reinvestment tenor | reinvest at ten years when the policy rate is at least half a point above neutral, at three years when half a point below, at five otherwise |
| R3 HQLA duration | a quarter of earning HQLA in ten-year bonds when the curve's slope (ten-year yield less the benchmark) is at its post-2008 median of `r num(L$params$slope_med, 2)` pp, an eighth more or less for each point above or below, within 0–50% |
| R4 payout | 70% of earnings while GDP grew last quarter and CET1 is above the 12.5% target, 30% otherwise |
| R5 unsecured growth | card and personal-loan growth 5 points a year faster while unemployment is falling and growth is above 1%, 5 points slower when unemployment has risen by more than a point over the year or GDP contracts |
| R6 asset swap | none of earning HQLA in asset-swapped bonds while the bond–swap spread is below 0.5 pp, a quarter at 1 pp, half at 1.5 pp or more |
| R7 liquidity buffer | bills released to an LCR of 170% in calm quarters, rebuilt to 185% after a quarter in which GDP contracted or the rand lost more than 15% over the year |

The parameters were set in advance as round numbers, not fitted to the episodes. Fitted on the same sixty paths, any rule would look better than it is, which is the backtesting equivalent of marking your own matric paper.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rules
#| fig-cap: "What each strategy adds to NGFB's ROE across the histories, split by whether the policy rate averaged higher or lower than today over the episode. Diamonds: the average over all episodes."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| code-summary: "Figure: rules in rising and falling rates"
rk <- c("R1 hedge ratio with the policy rate", "R2 reinvestment tenor with the policy rate", "R3 HQLA duration with the curve's slope",
        "R4 payout with growth and capital", "R5 unsecured growth with the labour market", "R6 asset swap with the bond-swap spread",
        "R7 liquidity buffer with stress", "All seven rules", "80% at 5 years", "50% at 10 years", "25% of HQLA in 10-year bonds",
        "25% of HQLA in asset-swapped 5-year bonds", "Buffer at an LCR of 170%", "Best static hedge ratio with hindsight")
rlab <- c("R1 hedge ratio", "R2 reinvestment tenor", "R3 HQLA duration", "R4 payout", "R5 unsecured growth", "R6 asset swap",
          "R7 liquidity buffer", "All seven rules", "Static: 80% hedge at 5 years", "Static: 10-year reinvestment",
          "Static: 25% of HQLA in 10-year bonds", "Static: 25% of HQLA asset-swapped", "Static: buffer at LCR 170%",
          "Hindsight: best static hedge ratio")
rd <- ld[rk, ]; rd$lab <- factor(rlab, levels = rev(rlab))
rr <- rbind(data.frame(lab = rd$lab, v = 1e4 * rd$d_roe_up, s = "Rates rose"), data.frame(lab = rd$lab, v = 1e4 * rd$d_roe_down, s = "Rates fell"))
ggplot() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_segment(data = rd, aes(x = 1e4 * d_roe_up, xend = 1e4 * d_roe_down, y = lab, yend = lab), colour = MUTE, linewidth = .6) +
  geom_point(data = rr, aes(v, lab, colour = s), size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = rd, aes(1e4 * d_roe_mean, lab), shape = 23, size = 3.4, fill = FG, colour = BG) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Rates rose` = WARN, `Rates fell` = ACCENT), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Timing the rate cycle pays nothing; premia pay either way",
       subtitle = "Change in three-year average ROE against the plan, bps, averaged over the episodes in each group",
       x = "bps of ROE", y = NULL) +
  theme_slate()
```

* **R1, the hedge ratio keyed on the level of rates, adds nothing:** `r bps(ld_n("R1 hedge ratio with the policy rate", "d_roe_mean"))` on average, with a 5th percentile of `r bps(ld_n("R1 hedge ratio with the policy rate", "d_roe_p5"))`. It gains when a high rate is followed by cuts and loses when rates keep rising, and in history the two came about equally often. The prize is real, since choosing the right static ratio for each episode with hindsight would have added `r bps(ld_n("Best static hedge ratio with hindsight", "d_roe_mean"))`, but the level of the policy rate does not reveal it. The rate cycle is the Comrades of forecasting: everybody has a split time, nobody has the finish.
* **R2, the reinvestment tenor keyed on rates, pays less than always going long:** `r bps(ld_n("R2 reinvestment tenor with the policy rate", "d_roe_mean"))` against `r bps(ld_n("50% at 10 years", "d_roe_mean"))` for ten years throughout. Every quarter spent at three or five years gives up term premium that the timing never wins back.
* **R3, HQLA duration keyed on the curve's slope, earns the most of any single rule, though not in every episode:** `r bps(ld_n("R3 HQLA duration with the curve's slope", "d_roe_mean"))` on average against `r bps(ld_n("25% of HQLA in 10-year bonds", "d_roe_mean"))` for a fixed quarter of HQLA in bonds, with a better CET1 trough at fair value (`r pct(ld_n("R3 HQLA duration with the curve's slope", "cet1_min_fv"))` against `r pct(ld_n("25% of HQLA in 10-year bonds", "cet1_min_fv"))`) for the same EVE risk. A steep curve pays more carry and tends to flatten as long yields fall, so buying duration when the slope is high collects the bond's excess return when it is largest, which is the term-premium evidence of @FamaBliss1987 and @CampbellShiller1991 in South African data. The catch is that R3 trades its book, and a bond sold out of an FVOCI book takes its accumulated gain or loss into profit. Curves flatten most often because the SARB is hiking, when long yields rise too, so R3 sells at a loss in hiking cycles: its realised losses average `r rmn(-r3_rise)` before tax over the episodes in which rates rose, against gains of `r rmn(r3_fall)` where they fell. It adds `r bps(ld_n("R3 HQLA duration with the curve's slope", "d_roe_up"))` when rates rise and `r bps(ld_n("R3 HQLA duration with the curve's slope", "d_roe_down"))` when they fall. Today's slope of `r num(L$params$slope_jo, 2)` pp is below its median, so the rule would start at `r pct(L$theta0, 0)` of HQLA, not a quarter.
* **R4, the payout keyed on growth and capital, adds a little and protects capital:** `r bps(ld_n("R4 payout with growth and capital", "d_roe_mean"))` with a CET1 trough of `r pct(ld_n("R4 payout with growth and capital", "cet1_min_fv"))`, above the plan's `r pct(ld_n("Plan", "cet1_min_fv"))`. A flat 70% payout adds `r bps(ld_n("70% payout", "d_roe_mean"))` but takes `r pct(ld_n("70% payout", "breach"), 0)` of the episodes below the 11.5% floor. Paying more when the economy grows and capital is ample, and less otherwise, keeps the capital where the downturns are.
* **R5, unsecured growth keyed on the labour market, does nothing here** (`r bps(ld_n("R5 unsecured growth with the labour market", "d_roe_mean"))`). The engine applies the industry's loss rate to the whole book, with no vintages, so the timing of origination cannot pay. A bank with its own vintage loss curves should run this test on them before concluding that credit timing is worthless.
* **R6 and R7 beat the plan in every episode, and take no rate risk.** A static quarter of HQLA in asset-swapped bonds adds `r bps(ld_n("25% of HQLA in asset-swapped 5-year bonds", "d_roe_mean"))` with a 5th percentile of `r bps(ld_n("25% of HQLA in asset-swapped 5-year bonds", "d_roe_p5"))`; R6 adds `r bps(ld_n("R6 asset swap with the bond-swap spread", "d_roe_mean"))`, because it holds little while the spread is as tight as today's. Releasing bills to an LCR of 170% adds `r bps(ld_n("Buffer at an LCR of 170%", "d_roe_mean"))`, and R7, which rebuilds the buffer after a stress signal (`r pct(L$stress_share, 0)` of the episodes' quarters), adds `r bps(ld_n("R7 liquidity buffer with stress", "d_roe_mean"))`. The difference between them is what the insurance costs.
* **All seven together add `r bps(ld_n("All seven rules", "d_roe_mean"))` on average** and beat the plan in `r pct(ld_n("All seven rules", "win"), 0)` of the episodes, lifting the share of histories in which NGFB earns its cost of equity from `r pct(ld_n("Plan", "coe_hit"), 0)` to `r pct(ld_n("All seven rules", "coe_hit"), 0)`. Most of that is duration, and so is most of the risk: a 200 bp rise would take a further `r pct(ld_n("All seven rules", "d_eve200"), 0)` of CET1 off the books' value, and the CET1 trough at fair value falls to `r pct(ld_n("All seven rules", "cet1_min_fv"), 2)`, a whisker above the floor. Seven rules stacked without a budget use more of the bank's risk capacity than anybody set out to give them.

## Choosing the levers together, under a risk budget

That last result is the wrong way round. An ALCO does not pick strategies and then discover how much risk they take. It sets a risk appetite and asks what earns the most inside it. So the question becomes: given a risk budget, which combination of levers earns NGFB the most across the histories?

The objective is NGFB's three-year average ROE, averaged over the `r RB$n_episodes` episodes with each history weighted equally:

$$\max_{x}\;\; \frac{1}{`r RB$n_episodes`}\sum_{e=1}^{`r RB$n_episodes`} \overline{\text{ROE}}_e(x) .$$

$x$ sets six decisions: the hedge ratio and the reinvestment tenor (chosen together, because they interact), the share of earning HQLA in ten-year bonds, the share in asset-swapped bonds, the size of the buffer, and the payout. Each can be fixed today or follow its macro rule. The limits must hold in every quarter $t$ of every episode $e$:

| Limit | Condition | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Tail | the 5th percentile of $\overline{\text{ROE}}_e(x)$ across the episodes is no worse than the plan's (`r pct(plan_p5)`) | a higher average bought with a worse bad case is a bet, not positioning |
| Capital | CET1, including the bonds' OCI reserve, at least 11.5% | the management floor, at fair value |
| Liquidity | LCR with HQLA at market value at least 120%; NSFR at least 110% | management floors above the 100% minima |
| Interest-rate risk | $\lvert \Delta\text{EVE}_{e,t}(x) - \Delta\text{EVE}_{e,t}(\text{plan})\rvert \le B$ of CET1, for a ±200 bp parallel shock | the plan is the bank's accepted position; $B$ bounds how far strategy moves it, in either direction |
| Liquidity book | ten-year bonds, asset swaps and released bills together at most 90% of earning HQLA | some bills stay for day-to-day liquidity management |

The EVE limit is relative to the plan for a practical reason. Without a behavioural model of the deposits' own economic value, the bank's total EVE is not measurable from public data, but the change a strategy makes to it is: that is the change in the value of the hedge and bond books. $B$ is the budget, and the central case sets it at `r pct(RB$b_central, 0)` of CET1.

| Lever | Settings | Options |
|---|---|---|
| Hedge ratio | `r paste(RB$levers$ratio, collapse = ", ")` | `r length(RB$levers$ratio)` |
| Reinvestment tenor | `r paste(RB$levers$tenor, collapse = ", ")` | `r length(RB$levers$tenor)` |
| Ten-year bonds (share of earning HQLA) | `r paste(RB$levers$duration, collapse = ", ")` | `r length(RB$levers$duration)` |
| Asset-swapped bonds (share of earning HQLA) | `r paste(RB$levers$asset_swap, collapse = ", ")` | `r length(RB$levers$asset_swap)` |
| Size of the buffer | the plan's (LCR `r pct(LV$lcr0, 0)`), `r paste(RB$levers$buffer[-1], collapse = ", ")` | `r length(RB$levers$buffer)` |
| Payout | `r paste(RB$levers$payout, collapse = ", ")` | `r length(RB$levers$payout)` |

That is $`r paste(lengths(RB$levers), collapse = " \\times ")`$ = `r format(RB$n_combos, big.mark = ",")` combinations. Running every one of them through the engine on every path would mean about `r num(RB$n_combos * RB$n_paths / 1e6, 1)` million engine runs, the strategic-planning equivalent of a queue at Home Affairs. It is also unnecessary, because of how the levers work:

1. **Each setting on its own.** Every setting of every lever runs through the engine with everything else at the plan, on every path: the `r RB$n_episodes` episodes, the three scenarios and the variant. That is `r RB$n_runs_per_path` runs per path. Each run keeps, quarter by quarter, net income, risk-weighted assets, the bond books' OCI reserve, the PV01 of the hedge and bond books, the LCR and the NSFR.
2. **A surrogate for every combination.** A combination's changes against the plan are added up quarter by quarter, because the levers act on different parts of the balance sheet: the hedge on NII, the bond books on NII and OCI, the buffer on HQLA and wholesale funding. The exception is the payout, which acts on every rand the other levers add, so equity is rolled forward with the combination's own payout:
$$\Delta\text{NI}_{e,t}(x) \;\approx\; \sum_{k} \Delta\text{NI}_{e,t}(x_k), \qquad E_{e,t}(x) \;=\; E_{e,t-1}(x) \;+\; \big(1-\pi_{e,t}(x)\big)\,\text{NI}_{e,t}(x) ,$$
where $\pi_{e,t}(x)$ is the payout ratio: a fixed number, or rule R4 reading the combination's own CET1 ratio. ROE, CET1 and the EVE ratio are then computed from that equity. The surrogate reproduces every single setting exactly, and on every combination checked against the full engine it is within `r num(1e4 * max(abs(RB$verify$roe_err)), 2)` bp of ROE.
3. **Score everything.** All `r format(RB$n_combos, big.mark = ",")` combinations are scored on every episode and quarter, with minima and percentiles taken after adding, and the best feasible one is kept at each EVE budget. There is no search heuristic to get stuck: the frontier is exact for the grid.
4. **Exact runs.** Every chosen combination is re-run through the full engine on every path, and the limits are checked on those runs, not on the surrogate.
5. **Out of sample.** The optimum is chosen on the first 25 episodes and scored on the last 25, and the other way round. The eleven episodes in between share quarters with both halves and are left out.

```{r}
#| label: fig-frontier
#| fig-cap: "The risk-budgeted frontier: the best change in NGFB's average ROE across the histories that meets every limit, at each EVE budget, with every setting allowed (rules included) and with static settings only. Dotted: the central budget."
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-summary: "Figure: the frontier"
fq2 <- fq; fq2$gain <- 1e4 * (fq2$roe - plan_roe); fq2$p5g <- 1e4 * (fq2$roe_p5 - plan_p5)
fq2$set <- ifelse(fq2$static_only, "Static settings only", "Every setting (rules allowed)")
ggplot(fq2, aes(100 * budget, gain, colour = set)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100 * RB$b_central, colour = MUTE, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = fq2[!fq2$static_only, ], aes(label = sprintf("%+.0f", gain)), colour = FG, size = 3.1, vjust = -1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Every setting (rules allowed)` = ACCENT, `Static settings only` = ACCENT2), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 100 * RB$budgets, labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 370)) +
  labs(title = "Most of the gain needs almost no interest-rate risk",
       subtitle = "Change in average ROE against the plan, bps, at each EVE budget",
       x = "EVE budget: largest change in EVE for ±200 bps against the plan's (% of CET1)", y = "bps of ROE") +
  theme_slate()
```

Most of the gain needs almost no EVE budget. With `r pct(RB$budgets[1], 0)` of CET1 the best combination already adds `r bps(fqb(.01) - plan_roe)`; at the central `r pct(RB$b_central, 0)` it adds `r bps(fqb(.05) - plan_roe)`, and the next five points of budget add only `r ubps(fqb(.10) - fqb(.05))` more. The reason is that the largest levers are spreads, not duration: the asset swap and the smaller buffer take no interest-rate risk at all. Beyond 10% of CET1 the frontier buys ROE with duration, and the tail starts to give: at 30% the average gain is `r bps(fqb(.30) - plan_roe)` but the 5th percentile gains only `r bps(fqb(.30, col = "roe_p5") - plan_p5)`, against `r bps(fqb(.10, col = "roe_p5") - plan_p5)` at 10%. Static settings alone come within `r ubps(fqb(.05) - fqb(.05, TRUE))` of the frontier at the central budget.

### The risk-budgeted portfolio

```{r}
#| label: numbers-rb
#| code-summary: "The central portfolio, from the exact runs"
vfy <- RB$verify; rownames(vfy) <- vfy$key
vc <- vfy[cen$key, ]; vs <- vfy[sta$key, ]
```

| | Plan | Risk-budgeted | Static settings only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hedge ratio | `r pct(N$hedge_ratio)` of non-maturity deposits | `r cen$hedge_ratio` | `r sta$hedge_ratio` |
| Reinvestment tenor | 5 years | `r cen$hedge_tenor` | `r sta$hedge_tenor` |
| Ten-year bonds in HQLA | none | `r cen$duration` of earning HQLA | `r sta$duration` |
| Asset-swapped bonds in HQLA | none | `r cen$asset_swap` of earning HQLA | `r sta$asset_swap` |
| Size of the buffer | LCR `r pct(LV$lcr0, 0)` | `r cen$buffer` | `r sta$buffer` |
| Payout | 50% | R4: 70% while GDP grows and CET1 is above 12.5%, 30% otherwise | `r sta$payout` |
| **Average ROE across the histories** | **`r pct(plan_roe)`** | **`r pct(plan_roe + cen$d_roe)`** (`r bps(cen$d_roe)`) | **`r pct(plan_roe + sta$d_roe)`** (`r bps(sta$d_roe)`) |
| 5th percentile of ROE | `r pct(plan_p5)` | `r pct(plan_p5 + cen$d_p5)` | `r pct(plan_p5 + sta$d_p5)` |
| Histories in which it beats the plan | – | `r pct(cen$win, 0)` | `r pct(sta$win, 0)` |
| NII over three years, average | `r rbn(RB$plan_row$nii, 1)` | `r rbn(vc$nii_exact, 1)` | `r rbn(vs$nii_exact, 1)` |
| CET1 at fair value, lowest quarter | `r pct(RB$plan_row$cet1_min, 2)` | `r pct(cen$cet1_min, 2)` | `r pct(sta$cet1_min, 2)` |
| LCR at market value, lowest quarter | `r pct(RB$plan_row$lcr_min, 0)` | `r pct(vc$lcr_exact, 0)` | `r pct(vs$lcr_exact, 0)` |
| EVE budget used (% of CET1) | 0% | `r pct(cen$eve_max)` | `r pct(sta$eve_max)` |

At a budget of `r pct(RB$b_central, 0)` of CET1 the optimiser keeps the hedge at the rate-neutral 37% of non-maturity deposits instead of the plan's `r pct(N$hedge_ratio)`, reinvests maturing tranches at seven years, holds 12.5% of earning HQLA in ten-year bonds and 50% in asset-swapped bonds, releases bills to an LCR of 160%, and pays out by rule R4. Across the histories NGFB's average ROE rises from `r pct(plan_roe)` to `r pct(plan_roe + cen$d_roe)`, the 5th percentile from `r pct(plan_p5)` to `r pct(plan_p5 + cen$d_p5)`, and the portfolio beats the plan in every one of the `r RB$n_episodes` episodes.

Two limits bind: the EVE budget (`r pct(cen$eve_max)` of the `r pct(RB$b_central, 0)`) and the cap on the liquidity book (`r pct(cen$use_max, 0)` of earning HQLA out of bills, against 90%). CET1 keeps `r ubps(cen$cet1_min - M$cet1_min)` above its floor in the worst quarter of the worst episode. Across all `r format(RB$n_combos, big.mark = ",")` combinations, the EVE budget rules out `r pct(RB$binds[["eve_central"]], 0)`, the CET1 floor `r pct(RB$binds[["cet1"]], 0)`, the tail `r pct(RB$binds[["tail"]], 0)` and the cap on the liquidity book `r pct(RB$binds[["hqla_cap"]], 0)`. The LCR and NSFR floors never bind for any combination, because the buffer's release runs out of wholesale funding to repay first.

In the named scenarios the same portfolio lifts NGFB's ROE by between `r bps(min(rbs$roe_central - rbs$roe_plan))` and `r bps(max(rbs$roe_central - rbs$roe_plan))`: from `r pct(rbs["baseline", "roe_plan"])` to `r pct(rbs["baseline", "roe_central"])` in the baseline and from `r pct(rbs["downside", "roe_plan"])` to `r pct(rbs["downside", "roe_central"])` in the downside. The downside is where it is tightest. Its CET1 trough at fair value falls from `r pct(rbs["downside", "cet1_plan"], 2)` to `r pct(rbs["downside", "cet1_central"], 2)`, because R4 pays out 70% of the higher earnings before the contraction arrives and the bond books lose value in the sovereign stress.

```{r}
#| label: fig-regime
#| fig-cap: "The risk-budgeted portfolio's change in ROE against the plan, lever by lever, averaged over the episodes in which the policy rate rose, stayed broadly flat or fell (by more than 25 bps on average). Interaction is mostly R4 paying out the other levers' earnings."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| code-summary: "Figure: where the ROE comes from"
lvl <- c(hedge = "Hedge ratio\nand tenor", dur = "Ten-year\nbonds", as = "Asset-swapped\nbonds", buf = "Smaller\nbuffer", pay = "Payout\n(R4)", interaction = "Interaction")
rgl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lvl), function(k) data.frame(lever = lvl[[k]], regime = rg$regime, v = 1e4 * rg[[k]])))
rgl <- rgl[rgl$regime %in% c("Rates rising", "Rates flat", "Rates falling"), ]
rgl$regime <- factor(rgl$regime, levels = c("Rates rising", "Rates flat", "Rates falling"), labels = c("rose", "flat", "fell"))
rgl$lever <- factor(rgl$lever, levels = lvl)
ggplot(rgl, aes(regime, v, fill = v >= 0)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = FG, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_col(width = .7, alpha = .92) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.0f", v), vjust = ifelse(v >= 0, -.4, 1.3)), colour = FG, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~lever, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ACCENT, `FALSE` = WARN), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-80, 100)) +
  labs(title = "A rate-neutral core and a macro-sensitive edge",
       subtitle = sprintf("bps of ROE against the plan. %d episodes with rates higher on average, %d flat, %d lower.",
                          rg["Rates rising", "n"], rg["Rates flat", "n"], rg["Rates falling", "n"]),
       x = "the policy rate over the episode, against today", y = "bps of ROE") +
  theme_slate() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

The portfolio has a rate-neutral core and a macro-sensitive edge.

* **The core is the two spread trades.** The asset swap adds `r bps(rg["All episodes", "as"])` and the smaller buffer `r bps(rg["All episodes", "buf"])`, and both add the same whether rates rise or fall, growth is strong or weak, or the episode holds a contraction. One collects the fiscal premium, the other the gap between wholesale funding and bills, and neither depends on the policy path. Together they are `r pct(spread_share, 0)` of the gain, and they use no EVE budget.
* **The edge is where the duration sits.** The plan holds its duration in the receive-fixed hedge. The optimiser moves part of it into government bonds: it cuts the hedge to the rate-neutral ratio and holds ten-year bonds and longer reinvestment instead, at a similar EVE, because a ten-year bond earns the fiscal premium on top of the term premium a swap earns. The two then offset each other across the rate cycle. The smaller hedge gains `r bps(rg["Rates rising", "hedge"])` when rates rise and loses `r ubps(rg["Rates falling", "hedge"])` when they fall; the bonds add `r bps(rg["Rates falling", "dur"])` when rates fall and `r bps(rg["Rates rising", "dur"])` when they rise. The whole portfolio adds `r bps(rg["Rates rising", "total"])` when rates rise and `r bps(rg["Rates falling", "total"])` when they fall.
* **The payout is the one macro rule that survives.** R4 adds `r bps(rg["All episodes", "pay"])` directly and most of the `r bps(rg["All episodes", "interaction"])` interaction, by paying out more of the other levers' earnings in good times. It adds least where growth is weak, which is the point: it keeps capital where the downturns are.

Why are the other rules not chosen? Under binding limits, a rule earns its place only if its signal predicts the premium it collects better than a fixed setting that uses the same room. R1 and R2 time the rate cycle, which the lab found does not pay. R3 earned the most of any single rule in the lab, but it trades its book: its realised losses in hiking cycles count against the tail limit, and its duration, and so the EVE budget it uses, peaks when the curve is steepest, so within a budget a fixed holding does better. R6 holds less than a fixed 50% while the spread is as tight as today's, and R7 holds more liquidity than a fixed 160% in stress quarters; both cost income under a cap that binds. The rules' value lies in what this engine does not price, R7's liquidity in a run and R6's sizing to spread risk. They belong in the ALCO's playbook as risk triggers rather than return engines.

The result leans on two things, and both are the bank's to set. **The liquidity book carries it:** with the hedge and payout left at the plan, the liquidity book alone adds `r bps(vr("Liquidity book only"))`, while with the liquidity book left in bills, the hedge and payout together add only `r bps(vr("Hedge and payout only"))`. **And it rests on the cap and the spread appetite:** the optimiser takes the spread trades to whatever limits it is given, because the engine prices neither the asset swap's spread risk beyond the modelled spread nor the liquidity a smaller buffer gives up. With the asset swap at most a quarter of HQLA and the LCR no lower than 170%, the gain is `r bps(vr("Asset swap at most 25%, LCR at least 170%"))`; with the liquidity book capped at 70% or 50% of earning HQLA, it is `r bps(vr("Liquidity book capped at 70% of HQLA"))` or `r bps(vr("Liquidity book capped at 50% of HQLA"))`. Those limits belong to the bank's credit-spread risk appetite and its own liquidity stress test, and the variants say what each is worth.

Out of sample, the portfolio chosen on the first 25 episodes (starting 2008Q2 to 2014Q2, which hold the 2008–09 cuts) is the full sample's, and on the last 25 it adds `r bps(RB$oos$roe_test[1])` against a best possible `r bps(RB$oos$roe_test_best[1])`. Chosen on the last 25 (starting 2017Q2 to 2023Q2, which hold the 2021–23 hiking cycle), the optimiser prefers a 20% hedge reinvested at ten years with 25% of HQLA in ten-year bonds, less receive-fixed and more bonds. On the first 25 that choice adds `r bps(RB$oos$roe_test[3])` against a best possible `r bps(RB$oos$roe_test_best[3])`. The rate-neutral core transfers between periods. How much duration to hold, and where, depends on which rate cycles the sample happens to contain, which is why that budget should be set explicitly rather than read off history.

## The lever that was missing

Before writing this up I went back through the optimiser's levers looking for an approach it had missed, something that would squeeze more NII or ROE out of the same strategy. Most candidates failed, and for reasons worth recording:

* **Issuing Additional Tier 1 or Tier 2 capital** would cheapen the total capital stack, but what binds in the downside is the CET1 floor, which neither instrument counts towards.
* **Pricing deposits harder** is already in the lever list as an upper bound (`r bps(lv("Deposit pricing", "10% less of rises, 10% more of cuts"))`), and without a measured volume response it cannot be sized honestly.
* **Terming out wholesale funding** for the NSFR needs a term premium on bank paper that public data do not publish.
* **Repo-ing the HQLA bonds** to release cash is economically the same trade as shrinking the buffer, which the optimiser already has.
* **Redeploying HQLA into lending** is ruled out at the margin by the positioning section: the plan is optimal under the baseline, and the static case for more lending is a franchise question.
* **Holding the bonds at amortised cost** instead of fair value changes reported CET1 volatility, not the economics, and HQLA count at market value in the LCR either way.
* **Options on rates** need a ZAR volatility surface that is not public.
* **A one-off capital distribution** competes with R4 for the same capital room, and inside the budget R4 uses it better.

One candidate survived, and it is the one resource every lever so far leaves alone: **the size of the balance sheet itself.** Every lever above rearranges the balance sheet NGFB already has. A rand of bills becomes a rand of bonds, a rand of bills repays a rand of wholesale funding, a rand of profit is paid out or kept. But a bank can also buy more government bonds than its liquidity buffer needs, asset-swap them exactly as above, and fund them in repo against the bonds themselves. That is how South African banks hold much of their sovereign book, and it was missing from the optimiser.

Funded in repo rather than by displacing bills, each rand of this carry book earns the bond–swap spread plus the floating leg, less the repo rate and the spread NGFB pays over it:

$$\text{carry}_t \;=\; bs \;+\; f_t \;-\; \big(r^{\text{repo}}_t + s^{\text{repo}}\big) ,$$

with $s^{\text{repo}}$ = `r num(100 * CY$repo_spread, 0)` bp, the spread NGFB already pays on its repo funding. At the jump-off that is `r num(CY$carry_jo, 2)` pp a year, about `r num(cyx$gap, 2)` pp less than the same bond earns inside the buffer, because the bills it would replace there yield below the policy rate while repo costs above it. What makes it interesting is what it does *not* use. It needs no HQLA, because the bonds are encumbered in the repo and secured funding against Level 1 collateral carries no LCR outflow. It needs no EVE budget, because the swap removes the rate risk. It needs almost no risk-weighted assets, because rand claims on the sovereign carry a zero risk weight, which leaves only the counterparty risk on the repo and the swap. It adds 5% of its size to required stable funding and all of it to the leverage exposure.

So it needs limits the optimiser did not have, and three are added. The **leverage ratio**, CET1 over on-balance-sheet assets (a conservative stand-in for Tier 1 over the full exposure measure), must stay at or above `r pct(CY$lr_floor, 0)`. South Africa's minimum is 4%, and from July 2025 a systemically important bank holds a further leverage buffer of half its higher-loss-absorbency requirement [@PA2025D3]. The **CET1 floor** must now hold in the named scenarios as well as in the replayed histories. And the book's **credit-spread risk** is measured: what a 100 bp widening of the bond–swap spread would take off the bond books, after tax, as a share of CET1,

$$\text{spread risk} \;=\; \frac{100 \times \text{spread PV01} \times (1-\tau)}{\text{CET1}} .$$

The carry book is then added to the central portfolio in steps of R25bn, with every other lever left where it was.

| Carry book | ROE against the plan | against the central portfolio | 100 bp spread widening (% of CET1) | CET1 trough, histories | CET1 trough, downside | Leverage ratio, lowest | Every limit met |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
`r paste(sprintf("| %s | %s | %s | %s | %s | %s | %s | %s |", cyt$carry, bps(cyt$d_roe), bps(cyt$d_roe_vs_central), pct(cyt$csrbb), pct(cyt$cet1_min, 2), pct(cyt$cet1_downside, 2), pct(lev_low, 2), ifelse(cyt$ok_scen, "yes", "**no**")), collapse = "\n")`

```{r}
#| label: fig-carry
#| fig-cap: "Adding a repo-funded book of asset-swapped bonds to the risk-budgeted portfolio. The leverage ratio never comes close to its floor; the stagflationary downside's CET1 trough is what stops the book at R50bn."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| code-summary: "Figure: the carry book"
cb <- cyt; cb$size <- c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100); cb$ok <- ifelse(cb$ok_scen, "within every limit", "breaks a limit")
p1 <- ggplot(cb, aes(size, 1e4 * d_roe_vs_central, fill = ok)) + geom_col(width = 16, alpha = .92) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * d_roe_vs_central)), colour = FG, size = 3.2, vjust = -.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`within every limit` = ACCENT, `breaks a limit` = WARN), name = NULL,
                    breaks = c("within every limit", "breaks a limit")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = cb$size) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 45)) +
  labs(title = "ROE added (bps)", x = "carry book (R bn)", y = NULL) + theme_slate() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 12))
p2 <- ggplot(cb, aes(size, 100 * cet1_downside)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 100 * M$cet1_min, colour = WARN, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 100 * M$cet1_min, label = "11.5% floor", colour = FG, size = 3, hjust = 0, vjust = 1.4) +
  geom_line(colour = ACCENT2, linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(colour = ACCENT2, size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = cb$size) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(11.35, 11.65), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = "CET1 trough, downside", x = "carry book (R bn)", y = NULL) + theme_slate() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12))
p3 <- ggplot(cb, aes(size, 100 * pmin(lev_min, lev_scen_min))) + geom_hline(yintercept = 100 * CY$lr_floor, colour = WARN, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 100 * CY$lr_floor, label = "5% floor", colour = FG, size = 3, hjust = 0, vjust = -.6) +
  geom_line(colour = INDIGO, linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(colour = INDIGO, size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = cb$size) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(4.8, 6.2), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = "Leverage ratio, lowest", x = "carry book (R bn)", y = NULL) + theme_slate() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12))
(p1 | p2 | p3) + plot_annotation(title = "Leverage is not the limit; the sovereign is",
  theme = theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = BG, colour = NA), plot.title = element_text(colour = FG, face = "bold", size = 14)))
```

Each R25bn of carry book adds about `r ubps(CY$per_step[["roe"]])` of ROE (`r rbn(CY$per_step[["nii"]], 1)` of NII over three years) and `r num(100 * CY$per_step[["csrbb"]], 1)` points of CET1 to the loss from a 100 bp spread widening. It earns that in every macro regime alike, as the asset swap inside the buffer does: the R100bn book adds `r bps(CY$regime$carry[CY$regime$regime == "Rates rising"])` when rates rise, `r bps(CY$regime$carry[CY$regime$regime == "Rates falling"])` when they fall and `r bps(CY$regime$carry[CY$regime$regime == "A contraction"])` in episodes with a contraction.

None of the limits the optimiser already had stops it. Even with R100bn added, the leverage ratio is `r pct(min(lev_low), 1)` at its lowest, and across the replayed histories the CET1 floor would not bind until well beyond the largest book tested. The leverage ratio, which looked like the obvious guard at the gate, turns out to be asleep in the guardhouse. History does hold spread widenings as large as the downside's (`r num(cyx$widen_hist, 2)` pp at the worst, in the episode that replays 2020, against `r num(cyx$widen_down, 2)` pp in the downside), but never at the same time as a deep contraction *and* rising rates. 2020's widening came with 300 bps of cuts, and 2015–16's with hikes but no deep recession, so in history the carry book's loss never landed on capital already thinned by credit losses and a hedge losing money. The stagflationary downside combines all three, and that is what binds: at R75bn its CET1 trough falls to `r pct(cyt["R75bn", "cet1_downside"], 2)`, below the floor. The largest book that keeps every limit in every history and every scenario is `r cyr$carry`. It lifts the central portfolio by `r bps(cyr$d_roe_vs_central)` to `r bps(cyr$d_roe)` against the plan, and raises the loss from a 100 bp spread widening from `r pct(CY$central_csrbb)` to `r pct(cyr$csrbb)` of CET1.

The lesson for the risk budget is worth more than the twenty basis points. A budget set only on EVE, on capital in replayed history and on liquidity barely sees a position whose risk is the sovereign spread. The carry book walked straight through all three, and only a scenario built around a fiscal shock stopped it. So it needs a limit of its own, a credit-spread budget in the banking book (CSRBB), and every point of CET1 put into that budget buys about `r ubps(CY$per_step[["roe"]] / CY$per_step[["csrbb"]] * 0.01)` of ROE. Whether that is a good price is a question about the sovereign, not about NGFB. The carry *is* the fiscal premium, and a bank that earns more of it is more exposed to exactly the event the premium pays for. Selling insurance is a lovely business until the claim comes in. In a banking system whose fortunes are already tied tightly to the sovereign's [@HesseMiyajima2022Nexus], that is not an abstract point.

## What didn't work and some health warnings

The standing rule holds. Everything that was tried and failed is declared, because the failure is informative and because a reader who tries the obvious thing should know where it leads.

Four of the failures are told in full above and need only a line here: **maximising the engine's ROE directly** (`r ubps(P$naive_gain)` of make-believe, replaced by reverse optimisation), **a swap curve inside the government curve** (`r ubps(corr["baseline", "d_roe"])` of ROE that was never there, replaced by actual fixings), **the SARB's broken all-share series** (replaced by the OECD index, with a tripwire in the build), and **macro rules that time the rate cycle or credit, or stack without a budget** (replaced by the risk budget). The rest are new.

**Drawing every product share from six banks.** That needs a covariance with 66 parameters from six observations, and produced implausible balance sheets. Drawing five business-line dimensions and splitting within lines fixed it.

**Carving NGFB out of the existing banks.** Taking NGFB's book from the reported banks distorted every peer group's history and share dynamics. Adding NGFB to the industry leaves the data untouched.

**The SARB coincident indicator as the activity measure for regimes.** It ran negative through 2025–26 while GDP grew, labelling an expansion a contraction. Regimes now use real GDP alone.

**Naive LCR run-off factors.** Fixed run-offs by deposit line, generous inflows and no encumbrance put NGFB's LCR at 1,090%, a number that would make a treasurer smug and a regulator suspicious. Depositor-weighted Basel factors, calibrated to the published sector ratio, bring it to 190%.

**An outlier left in the calibration window.** One quarter of BA120 call-deposit cost at 10.5% pushed the solved wholesale spread to −0.26 pp over JIBAR, a funding spread nobody has ever been offered. Replacing it with the window median gives +1.17 pp.

**Monthly interest annualised by twelve.** A month's interest times twelve reads every February, with its 28 days of interest, as a 0.31 pp fall in savings-deposit costs, so every year the models celebrated a February rate cut that nobody had announced. The month's own day count removes the artefact.

And the health warnings, of which there are more than usual.

**Public data only.** Prices, losses and costs are the sector's, and NGFB differs from the sector only through its mix and its hedge. The relative loss multipliers by product are an external assumption normalised to the sector's loss ratio, because no return publishes losses by product. A real bank would replace the industry pricing with its own and the multipliers with its own loss history.

**The level of ROE rests on a few inputs.** The swap rates moved the baseline by `r ubps(corr["baseline", "d_roe"])`, and the level of credit losses is where the industry models carry the most model risk. The differences between scenarios, and the positioning, are much less sensitive to either.

**The swap curve does not price each scenario's path.** Swap rates are the benchmark plus constant term spreads, so receive-fixed swaps look slightly cheap in scenarios with cuts and dear in scenarios with hikes. With a curve that prices half of the coming path the conclusions stand: R1 still adds nothing (`r bps(L$dist$d_roe_mean[L$dist$phi == 0.5 & L$dist$strategy == "R1 hedge ratio with the policy rate"])`), and the gains from the tenor rule and a higher static ratio barely move, because they come from the term premium and today's swap rate, not from timing.

**History is one history.** The `r RB$n_episodes` overlapping windows hold about five or six independent three-year periods, one global financial crisis and one pandemic. The tail limit is the 5th percentile of those, which is the fourth-worst episode.

**The optimiser takes unpriced risks to their limits.** The asset swap's spread risk enters only through the modelled spread, and a smaller buffer's cost only through the LCR and NSFR, neither of which stresses run-offs or funding spreads. So both go to whatever caps they are given, and the caps are judgement.

**The carry book's funding is assumed to roll.** Repo is priced at NGFB's calibrated spread over the policy rate in every quarter. In a market dislocation like March 2020 repo haircuts and rates jump, and the book's real backstop is the SARB's lending facilities at a penalty rate. The engine prices neither.

**The bond–swap spread rests on three years of swap data,** a period in which the spread mostly compressed. A sovereign shock could move it more than a quarter of the long bond's move, which is why the spread risk is also measured at a flat 100 bp.

**Execution costs size the positioning moves.** Their direction is robust; their size scales with an assumption about how expensive it is to move a franchise inside a year.

**No second-round effects.** The scenarios are exogenous: NGFB's actions do not move prices or the macro path, and the sector does not respond to NGFB.

**ZARONIA is modelled at the fallback, not contract by contract.** In practice loans and notes follow their own fallback clauses and re-papering, and the quarter in which each contract switches is not known from public data.

**NGFB's hedge is not re-optimised for the refined deposit models.** The rate-neutral `r pct(A$neutral_ratio, 0)` is a finding about the canonical bank, not a recommendation for a real one.

---

## What ALCO does on Monday

1. **Fund the two spread trades first.** Asset-swapped government bonds and a smaller buffer add about `r ubps(rg["All episodes", "as"] + rg["All episodes", "buf"])` of ROE in every macro regime, with no rate view and no EVE cost. Size them against a credit-spread limit and the bank's own liquidity stress test, not against the LCR.
2. **Hold duration in bonds, not only in swaps.** At the same EVE, a government bond earns the fiscal premium on top of the term premium a swap earns. Keep the structural hedge near its rate-neutral ratio and let the bond book and the reinvestment tenor carry the duration the budget allows.
3. **Make the payout state-contingent.** R4 is the one macro rule that survives the risk budget.
4. **Use the other macro rules as risk triggers, not return engines.** The slope, the bond–swap spread and the stress signals say when the premia are large and when liquidity is worth more. Under binding limits they do not beat fixed settings on return.
5. **Set the budgets explicitly, and price them.** At `r pct(RB$b_central, 0)` of CET1 the portfolio adds `r bps(cen$d_roe)`; the frontier says what each further point of EVE budget is worth, and the carry book says what a point of credit-spread budget is worth.
6. **Position ahead of a scenario in proportion to conviction, and read the regret matrix before the gain.** The credit leg of a downside positioning is robust to the SARB's response. The rate leg is a bet on it.
7. **Push where the market grows and NGFB does not.** Cards, corporate lending and vehicle finance in easing cycles, with their own deposits behind them; tighter card underwriting when GDP turns. Then judge the result against macro par, not against last year.

## The end of this one

The deposit series ended by pricing something it could not estimate. This one ends somewhere similar. The macro view matters enormously to what NGFB earns: its plan swings from `r pct(min(pl$roe))` to `r pct(max(pl$roe))` across sixty-one histories, and two macro numbers explain `r pct(L$drivers_r2, 0)` of that spread. But mattering is not the same as being tradeable. Keying the hedge to the level of rates earned nothing. Positioning ahead of a downside recovered `r pct(gain["downside", "downside"] / -att("downside"), 0)` of the damage and cost more than twice as much if the upside arrived instead. The one rule that survived a risk budget was a payout that pays more when the economy grows, which is less a forecast than good manners.

What did pay was dull. Collecting the fiscal premium without its duration, and not paying wholesale rates to hold bills nobody needs, added about a point and a half of ROE whatever the history, and the risk budget turned a pile of good ideas into a portfolio that beat the plan in every one of the `r RB$n_episodes` histories. The missing lever added another `r ubps(cyr$d_roe_vs_central)`, and a lesson worth more than the basis points: a risk budget that only sees rates, capital and liquidity will let a sovereign-spread position walk straight through it.

This ran on a bank that does not exist, with industry models I have deliberately not shown you, so I cannot tell you what it would do to yours. What I can say is that the shape of the answer is unusually robust. The spread trades paid in every history and every scenario. The rate bets did not. A treasury that sets its budgets explicitly, funds the premia that need no view, and keeps its rate views for the occasions it genuinely has one, should not need a crystal ball to earn its cost of equity more often than once in sixty-one tries.

*No refunds, as the man selling coat hangers at the robot will tell you: none of this is advice, and your own bank's risk budget should be set by people who can see its books.*
